title: A branch declares a set of specs, and the gate grades every one of them
deliverable: The branch's spec answer stops being a scalar. SpecFacts.written is already string[] and survives touchedWriteRegion as a set; specToGrade collapses it, and specToGrade, authoredAsPlan and specAddsClauseId exist only to make that choice. Delete all three, carry the set through to BranchStanding, and read it from the records this branch's store diff changed rather than from the event log -- which loses no evidence, because every WORK_OP writes the record a store diff would show. Then grade every declared spec rather than one chosen among them, and grade a branch on the clauses its own members discharge rather than on every clause in their specs, which is what makes merge-ready's spec and clauses legs meaningful on a branch holding one member of a multi-member spec instead of red-by-design.
evidence: Ruled by the author 2026-08-08 after the scalar chokepoint was measured: mergeReady.ts:265 (set), :256 (collapse), :57 (scalar). The red-by-design half is first-hand: the orchestrator brief for this push instructs the reader to expect the spec and clauses legs to fail legitimately on a multi-member branch, and that fired on two of Phase 3's three branches -- brief-builds-the-manifest and dropped-and-failed-clauses-differ.

title: A branch knows which spec it owes
evidence: The author reports the inference is wrong about half the time (2026-08-06 notes). merge-ready grades the spec it infers, so a wrong inference grades the wrong contract -- and with three branches in flight under an orchestrator, the wrong one is likely to be another live branch's rather than nothing. Prior art: spec-and-read-verbs-scope (done) narrowed inference to where a spec is used and named the near miss, and no-store-inference-on-main (done) stopped main inferring from the store, so this is the third pass and the remaining error should be characterised before it is fixed. merge-ready already prefers a spec the branch owes over a plan it merely wrote and names which it graded and how it got there, so the report exists; what is missing is the inference being right.

title: A spec whose file is present but whose Deliverable/Proof section becomes unparseable (bad merge, stray conflict markers, a mangled heading) while it is genuinely owed and untouched by any branch reads as "authored as plan" and is silently exempted from the spec and clauses legs
deliverable: Either specClausesDiffer/clauseIdsDiffer treats a clause count that dropped to zero on head (versus a nonzero base) as something other than ordinary authorship — e.g. unmet/unknown rather than a plan — or doctor's specIssues gains a check that a spec's parsed clause count did not collapse relative to its own recorded audit-pass clause ids while members remain open, so a corrupted-but-present spec fails loud instead of exempting the branch that broke it
evidence: Reproduced directly against the exported functions with a temp git repository: committed a-spec.md with two tagged clauses on main, then on a feature branch overwrote the same path with unresolved merge-conflict markers and no parseable "## Deliverable" section (the file still exists, so existsSync-based checks pass). specClausesDiffer(config, 'main', headSha, 'a-spec') returned true (0 parsed clauses on head versus 2 on base), and authoredAsPlan([{state:'open'}], true) returned true — the spec reads as an authored plan and merge-ready's spec/clauses legs are skipped with "No other spec was graded." doctor's specIssues(config) on the same tree returned an empty array: it only reports duplicate clause ids or an unreadable file, neither of which fires here, so nothing else in the merge gate catches it. This is exactly the "spec file that does not parse" seam the spec's own decisions call for a defensible verdict on, and the verdict produced is the accidental exemption the spec explicitly says must not happen. Outright deletion of the same file is caught separately, because checkStore's specExists(existsSync) check fails doctor with an error in that case — corruption-without-deletion is the gap.

title: touchedWriteRegion (decideSpec's c7 discriminator) trusts a task's declared `writes` grant as a stand-in for "this branch's diff did work against the spec," but the repository's own workflow (workPrompt.ts) documents that a diff diverging from its declared writes later is sanctioned, not a violation — so a spec with a stale or incomplete grant can be dropped as a candidate and merge-ready passes with no spec graded even though real, undeclared work landed
deliverable: touchedWriteRegion needs a signal beyond the stored writes grant before it drops a spec — for example, falling back to "touched" whenever this branch is the one that most recently wrote store events against the spec and has any commits at all (matching the existing fail-open polarity used when git cannot answer), or adding a doctor/merge-ready check that flags a branch whose diff falls outside every open task's declared writes for its own active spec as a stale-grant warning rather than staying silent
evidence: Reproduced directly with a temp git repository and the exported changedFiles/diffTouchesRegion functions, mirroring branchStanding's own region construction (specFile(spec) plus membersOf(spec).flatMap(task => task.writes)): committed a-spec.md and scripts/other-decl.ts on main (the latter standing in for the task's declared writes grant), then on a feature branch committed real work at scripts/actual-file.ts instead — a path the grant never named, and the spec file itself was never touched, which is the ordinary case since most implementation work does not hand-edit the spec markdown. changedFiles reported only scripts/actual-file.ts, and diffTouchesRegion(changed, ['specs/a-spec.md', 'scripts/other-decl.ts']) returned false. In decideSpec this spec is filtered out of `touched` before it can ever be graded, so if it were the branch's only candidate the gate reports "this branch is working no spec, so it owes no clause" over real, unaudited work. This branch's own task record needed exactly this kind of grant correction mid-flight (commit b31f0d5, "Correct the write grant"), so drift between a declared grant and the real diff is not a hypothetical here.

title: A brand-new, not-yet-populated spec reads as owed rather than as the plan it is
deliverable:
Either accept that a not-yet-populated spec is graded as owed and record that the choice was
deliberate, since it currently reads as coincidental, or give specClausesDiffer a way to read "absent from
base and still empty on head" as differing the same way "absent from base and now populated" already
does, so a freshly scaffolded plan is not asked to pass an audit over zero clauses before it can be
recognised as a plan.
evidence:
specClausesDiffer compares an absent-from-base clause set, empty, against a head clause set that
also happens to be empty when a spec file has been freshly created but not yet populated with a Proof
list. clauseIdsDiffer([], []) reads two empty sets as identical, so clausesDiffer is false, and
authoredAsPlan requires clausesDiffer===true to grant the plan exemption — so an all-open,
freshly-scaffolded, not-yet-authored spec is graded as a contract this branch owes rather than as the plan
it plainly is, and merge-ready's clauses leg then fails demanding an audit pass over a document with
nothing in it yet. Verified directly by calling clauseIdsDiffer([], []) (returns false) and
authoredAsPlan(open-members, false) (returns false) through the repository's own module resolution. This
is on the safe side pass 1 asked to be favoured — it blocks rather than waves through — so I am filing it
as non-blocking, but it is a real, reachable misclassification: a spec entering `written`
(specsWrittenFromBranch) before its Proof list is authored, for example immediately after a member is
scaffolded against the spec but before the spec doc itself is filled in, hits exactly this path.
reason: Accepted as deliberate, not a defect. A spec absent from base and still empty on head has no clause id for head to lack, so headAddsClauseId reads it as owed rather than as a plan -- the coordinator's ruling on finding 1 (grade the plan exemption on whether head adds an id, not on a symmetric difference) explicitly disposes of this: pure absence of content is not evidence of authorship any more than pure deletion is, and erring toward grading (demanding an audit) is the safe direction the spec asks for. A freshly-scaffolded, not-yet-authored spec earns its plan exemption once a real clause is written, which is the same trigger that already exempts any other brand-new spec.

title: Pass 1's finding 1 is only closed for total corruption, not partial
deliverable:
specClausesDiffer's corruption guard, the headClauses.length===0 and baseClauses.length>0
check, needs to catch partial clause loss from a mangled document, not only total loss, so a spec that is
genuinely owed and untouched but happened to get corrupted by a bad merge cannot exempt itself from the
gate by losing only some of its clauses instead of all of them. One direction: also refuse the exemption
whenever the deliverable section shows signs of not having been intentionally authored, such as a missing
Proof marker, literal merge-conflict-marker text inside the section, or a clause id present in the last
recorded audit pass's verdicts that silently vanished from the head parse with no new id replacing it.
evidence:
specClausesDiffer refuses the plan exemption only when the head copy parses to exactly zero clauses
against a populated base. A merge or rebase that leaves stray conflict-marker text over one bullet in the
middle of a Proof list, one of the three corruption causes pass 1's own finding named, drops that one
clause from the scan while leaving the rest intact, so headClauses.length is nonzero and the guard never
fires. The id-set comparison then reads the reduced set as differing from base, indistinguishable from an
intentional edit, and if every member is still open the spec reads as an authored plan again. Reproduced
directly with a temporary git repository against the exported branchStanding and specClausesDiffer
functions: base commit has a-spec.md with three tagged clauses (c1, c2, c3) and one open member whose
writes grant includes impl.ts; the feature-branch commit overwrites the middle bullet's line with literal
conflict-marker text while leaving the Deliverable heading, the Proof marker, and the other two bullets
intact. specClausesDiffer(config, main, resolveCommit(main), a-spec) returns true rather than null, and
branchStanding(config, main) reports spec a-spec, specAuthoredHere true. Before this whole branch existed,
the old file-existence check could not have produced this outcome for a file that already existed on
base, corrupted or not, because it never looked at clause content at all — this is a new failure mode this
branch's clause-identity approach introduced, of which pass 1 caught only the boundary case. doctor's
specIssues does not catch it either; it only flags duplicate clause ids or an unreadable file. I believe
this branch should not merge without addressing this: it is the same defect class pass 1 filed as HIGH,
reopened through a narrower door the fix did not anticipate.

title: A clause can be deferred, and a spec can carry its goal
evidence: A clause stands met, unmet or unknown. There is no way to say a branch deliberately dropped one, so the honest moves are to leave it outstanding -- which blocks merge-ready's spec leg forever -- or to edit the spec, which rewrites the contract silently and leaves the audit grading something nobody promised. Measured in this planning session: adding c8 to reimplement-localization shifted every clause after it and required rewiring --discharges across three task records by hand, with nothing checking the result; a fumble there would have left a clause owed by nobody and merge-ready would have passed a branch that dropped scope. The task-goal half comes from the author's notes (2026-08-06): task growth is recurring and usually not scope drift, because knowledge grows once a worker finishes its first round, and there is often a gap between a spec's clauses and the spirit of the task -- the audit-prompt-brief task had specific clauses while the actual goal was to settle the audit prompt, which nobody could have foreseen when writing it. Auditors already make evidence-based value judgements, so a recorded goal gives them something to judge against. Both halves are one problem: a contract written before the knowledge exists needs an honest way to record what was learned.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 2: A deferral must carry its reason. Recording `deferred` with no evidence is refused, because a deferral with no reason is an `unmet` clause with a shrug, and the one thing this must not become is a cheaper way to say unmet.

evidence: The truly-empty case is refused correctly (`--proof 1=deferred --evidence 1=` exits 1 with "clause 1 is deferred with no reason"), and the interactive walk correctly rejects a whitespace-only answer via `.trim() || null` (scripts/tasks/audit.ts:894). title: c1's proof grep catches a third file, this branch's own scripts/lib/realGitRepo.ts, so the recorded proof no longer returns what the record says it returns
deliverable: c1's boundary is stated as a rule the command expresses, rather than as a list of files to subtract. The rule the three exceptions actually share is "a module whose job is to build or model a repository is not a production read" — a grep scoped to the production command surface, or one exclusion naming that class once, restores the property that a later pass re-running the recorded proof gets the recorded answer. A fourth `grep -v` buys one commit.
evidence: Run at e364093, the clause's proof command verbatim -- `grep -rn "spawnSync('git'\|execFileSync('git'" scripts/tasks scripts/lib --include="*.ts" | grep -v "\.test\.ts" | grep -v "lib/git.ts" | grep -v "realGitFixture.ts"` -- returns `scripts/lib/realGitRepo.ts:15` and exits 0. Pass 2 recorded this same command as returning nothing (exit 1) at 5987dd8; 8a2d00e added realGitRepo.ts afterwards. This is the third recurrence of one pattern: pass 1 filed it for realGitFixture.ts (closed by 6934f36, which added an exclusion) and again for sourceFiles.ts (closed by routing that file through the seam), and the fix each time was to subtract one more name. The clause's substance is intact -- realGitRepo.ts is a test helper owned by Testing procedure, not a task-system production read -- so what is broken is the evidence chain, not the routing: an auditor who re-runs the recorded proof gets a different answer than the record, and the spec becomes history the moment this branch merges.

title: the identity initRealGitRepo writes is unproven on any machine that has a global git identity, which is every machine except CI
deliverable: One case in scripts/lib/git.test.ts that builds a repository through `initRealGitRepo` and commits with `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` and `GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM` pointed at the null device, asserting the commit lands and the author is the written one. That is the environment CI actually runs in, and it makes the optimization prove itself where it matters instead of being covered by the developer's own `~/.gitconfig`.
evidence: 8a2d00e replaced two `git config` spawns per repository with an append to `.git/config`, and that append survives a whole-suite mutation: replacing it with `void dir;` leaves 0 failed of 1863. The reason is that a developer machine's global identity answers instead. The written identity is in fact correct -- probed by hand, `git init -q -b main` plus the same append, then `git add`/`git commit` with GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM set to the null device, exits 0 with author `Test <test@example.com>` -- and .github/workflows/test.yml sets no git identity, so CI is the only thing standing behind it. A regression there surfaces as every real-git test in seven files failing at once for a reason none of them names.

title: the unborn-HEAD guard at context.ts:117 can be neutered with the whole suite green, because the parse catch below it returns the same answer
deliverable: Either the guard goes, since `parseStore` throwing on a null already produces the empty result through the catch at context.ts:121-123, or it is given an outcome the catch cannot produce so a test can tell them apart. Today it is a line the suite cannot distinguish from its own absence, which is the state the pass-2 finding was closed to leave behind.
evidence: Replacing `if (committedText === null) return [];` with `if (committedText === undefined) return [];` -- so the guard never fires -- SURVIVED at whole-suite scope, 0 failed of 1863. The behaviour the clause names is covered: replacing the same line with a fabricated working-tree-only warning is KILLED by doctor.test.ts "doctor degrades to no working-tree-comparison issue when there is no committed store (unborn HEAD)". The difference between the two mutations is the finding: the new test proves that doctor stays quiet under an unborn HEAD, which is what c5 asked for, and does not prove that this line is what keeps it quiet.

title: unbornDefaultStoreFixture's DataGit answers branch() and lsFiles() the way a born repository does, so the fake diverges from real git exactly where the fixture is named for
deliverable: DataGit's unborn form answers the two facts the way the seam's own realGit does: `branch()` null while `this.commits` is empty, and `lsFiles()` an empty array rather than null. Then a test written on this fixture measures a model real git agrees with, and `trackedFiles()` returns the empty list instead of throwing. The general form is that any fact DataGit answers unconditionally is a claim about git that nothing checks -- `mergeInProgress: () => false` is the other one -- so the fix worth having is a case in cliFixtures.test.ts that pins the unborn answers against the probe below.
evidence: cliFixtures.ts:217-229 documents the unborn form as "every revision read answers null, as git does before a branch's first commit". That is true of the revision reads and false of two others. Probed against real git (`git init -q -b main` in an empty dir with one untracked file): `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` exits 128, so the seam's `branch()` answers null, while DataGit's `branch: () => this.branchName` (cliFixtures.ts:236) answers 'main' unconditionally; `git ls-files` exits 0 with empty output, so the seam's `lsFiles()` answers `[]`, while DataGit's `lsFiles: () => (this.tip === null ? null : ...)` (cliFixtures.ts:282) answers null. The second one has teeth now that scripts/lib/sourceFiles.ts:17 throws on a null `lsFiles()`: the next test written on unbornDefaultStoreFixture that reaches an architecture command gets an exception where the real thing returns an empty list. Nothing is wrong today -- doctor consults neither fact -- which is what makes it a trap rather than a bug. This branch's whole argument is that a faked seam may stand in for the real one; a fake that is wrong in the state it is named for is how a green run stops meaning the tree is green in a new way.

title: A later pass converts what an earlier one filed, and a restated clause is reported
deliverable: The two adjacent confusions on the filing side of the audit.ts seam. cmdAudit's duplicate guard runs above the branch that sets the deferred shape, so a clause pass N graded unmet and pass N+1 grades deferred keeps spec set to the slug -- deferral converting rather than deleting is the feature's central promise and it fails on the second grading of a clause, which is the common case. And a pass that grades a clause unmet already creates an undelivered record for it, so an auditor that also files a --finding restating the same fault produces two records with nothing relating them: run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks pass 1 made six records for three faults, caught only by reading the member list by hand.
evidence: a-later-pass-grading-a-clause-deferred-cannot-convert-the-un (medium) and an-auditor-s-finding-that-restates-an-unmet-clause-makes-two (medium), both declined into dropped-and-failed-clauses-differ on 2026-08-07. Their recorded locators (audit.ts:1130 and :1126) predate audit-splits-at-its-seam; at head the record-creation block is scripts/tasks/audit.ts:493-525 and the duplicate guard sits above it. Split off the parent record because audit.ts is brief-builds-the-manifest's grant this round.

title: a later pass grading a clause deferred cannot convert the unmet record an earlier pass already created
deliverable: cmdAudit skips creating a record when one with the base id is already open, which correctly stops a re-graded unmet clause from duplicating itself. But the skip runs before the deferred branch, so a clause that pass N graded unmet and pass N+1 grades deferred keeps a record with spec set to the slug, when the deferred shape is spec null. The pass then reads deferred while the record still reads as an owed member of the spec, and the only way to reconcile is spec done --defer-open or an edit by hand. Deferral converting rather than deleting is the feature's own central promise, and it does not hold on the second grading of a clause, which is the common case since deferral is usually proposed after a clause has failed once.
evidence: Read at scripts/tasks/audit.ts:1126-1131 while closing run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks. The guard is if (tasks.some(task => task.id === baseId && task.state === 'open')) continue, placed above the block that sets spec to null for a deferred verdict. a-clause-can-be-deferred-and-a-spec-can-carry-its-goal's own Decisions section states the invariant this breaks: a deferral converts, it does not delete, and converting to undelivered keeps the promise visible and the work findable. Not hit on this spec, because pass 2 graded c2/c3/c5 unmet rather than deferred, but it would have been hit had any of the three been deferred.
reason: Folded into the push's branch that owns the file each one lives in: the first two into dropped-and-failed-clauses-differ, the trimming fix into brief-builds-the-manifest (its one-commit fix survives as tag archive/festive-blackburn-e1a2d4), and the shared-append-point into every-system-owns-its-files-by-name, which sorts every paths array so two branches adding a file merge line by line.

title: A lesson can be retired, and the retirement is recorded
deliverable: Removing an instruction from a brief becomes an operation that records what left and why, rather than a deletion from an array. Today briefLessons.ts's own header says to retire a lesson by deleting it and letting its citations resolve to nothing - and unknownLessonIds, the function that would report those citations, has no caller anywhere, so the stated retirement path is literally the silent drop c6 refuses. Same shape one table over as a record leaving docs/tasks.jsonl with nothing in the log able to say that it did; a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded is the spec to model on and the two should not invent different answers.
evidence: Author's observation 2026-08-06: lessons have no removal verb. Confirmed by reading: the four lesson arrays are edited by hand and nothing records a departure. The seam was found the same day from the other direction by the lesson-handle worker, which filed c6-s-reporting-half-is-a-capability-with-no-caller-so-a-dead after grepping the whole tree for callers of unknownLessonIds and finding none. Depends on the recurrence slice for the record-and-occurrence shape rather than inventing a second one.

It is the sole owner of c13 and the only medium member of the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place, and it is the one clause whose absence costs nothing while the system is frozen: no lesson gets retired if no branch is editing lessons. c13 is abandoned rather than deferred, because deferred says a later branch owes it and the freeze means no later branch is coming.

title: A lesson has a handle that survives rewording it
deliverable: Each of the nineteen instructions in the four brief lists gains a stable handle a record can cite, and the handle survives editing the instruction's own prose. The invariant, not the mechanism: renaming or rewording a lesson must not orphan the records citing it, and a citation naming no live lesson must be reported rather than silently dropped. Whether that is an added id field on Lesson or the array name plus an index is this task's call, made after reading how the nineteen hardcoded per-instruction assertions in briefLessons.test.ts are written - they are the reason the file resists a loop, and the same reason should decide the handle.
evidence: Third element of the channel, ruled 2026-08-06: a record may name the lesson it breaches, which turns 'how many defects' into 'which lesson is not landing' - the actionable form, because a lesson breached repeatedly is badly worded, in the wrong brief, or wrong, and each is fixable by editing one line. The information already exists: an auditor finding a test that cannot fail IS a breach of a worker lesson, and a fix-the-neighbour instance IS a breach of an auditor lesson. Only the pointer is missing. Independent of the fault field, so this runs beside the record-shape task rather than after it. Worth reading while here, not in this grant: MAX_LESSON_COUNT is 24 with 19 used, which is a quota of the same shape as the 5 percent comment budget CLAUDE.md retired on 2026-07-28, and the orchestrated run alone produced more than five lessons worth carrying.

title: A lesson is folded from its own log
deliverable: An append-only log whose events carry enough to apply, and a pure t-ordered fold that turns them into current state, built once on the nineteen lessons because that is the smallest real set in the repository. The four exported arrays in briefLessons.ts are deleted and become a genesis import; the briefs render from the fold and a test asserts the rendered output is byte-identical to what the arrays produced. FIRST THING TO ASK, before any code: the briefLessons.ts collision named in the spec's own Open questions is unresolved and is the author's call.
evidence: Adopted 2026-08-06 from a planning session in another context, verified before adoption rather than taken on report. The ordering argument rests on four measurements and all four were re-derived against the tree: 1606 events, zero null heads, 338 distinct heads, 51 of them outside HEAD's reachability, and 5 heads carrying events from more than one branch. Unreachable objects are what git gc prunes, so an ancestry-ordered fold decays; t is arrival order because every agent here runs on one machine. NOT STARTED: task-system work is frozen in favour of the MVP roadmap as of this session, and this record exists so the spec lands as a plan for a later branch rather than as a debt.

title: A move never strands a question
deliverable: A record waiting on an unanswered question cannot leave the queue silently. promote, defer, decline, start and done each warn, naming the question, before they move it -- never refuse, because the mover is usually the person answering. The guard goes where the state transition is assembled rather than into the five verbs one at a time, which is the same lesson this repository has now filed under three different names. Fold in nothing-routes-a-deferred-record-back-to-the-unreviewed-queu, which is the inverse route and the reason a question answered late has nowhere to land, and the-every-bounded-command-surface-test-hardcodes-its-list-so, whose hardcoded list is why three verbs went unswept and is a test that cannot fail for the reason it exists.
evidence: every-triage-action-has-a-non-interactive-form-pass3-asking- (high, open, reproduced three ways on head); nothing-routes-a-deferred-record-back-to-the-unreviewed-queu (medium); the-every-bounded-command-surface-test-hardcodes-its-list-so (medium). an-answered-question-record-is-stranded-when-any-verb-moves- was declined into the first as a duplicate on 2026-08-07.

title: A multi-word section heading is diagnosed as an unexpected line in the section, not as a bad heading
deliverable: The heading parser reports a heading whose id carries whitespace as what it is — an id must be one token — rather than falling through to the section body and blaming the heading line for being in the wrong place.
evidence: '# test records again' loads with 'both:21:1 [both] parse: unexpected line in # test: "# test records again"'. The line is a heading, at column 1, and the message names it as a line inside the preceding section, so the reader is pointed at the section above rather than at the two-word id. Hit while writing a fixture module for scripts/migrate-saves.test.ts; cost one round trip to diagnose from a message that had all the information and pointed the wrong way.

title: A mutation that turns tests into skips rather than failures is invisible to the shortfall check
deliverable: Compare what actually ran, not the denominator. parseVitestTally reads total out of the trailing (N), which counts skipped tests, and verdictOf's shortfall compares run.total against baseline.total. Baseline already carries ran = failed + passed for the -t typo refusal; the run has the same number and nothing compares it. A shortfall computed on ran would report the case total cannot see.
evidence: Measured on vitest 4.1.9 while establishing this branch's clauses. A suite whose beforeAll throws reports 'Tests 2 failed | 2 skipped (4)': the two tests under the broken hook are skipped, not failed, and total is unchanged. So a mutation that stops tests from running by breaking their setup produces no shortfall note, and the row reads as an ordinary measurement over a suite that partly did not run. The suite-level FAIL line makes this kill rather than survive today, which hides the gap; a mutation that skips tests without failing the suite would not be caught at all.

title: A mutation verdict names the test that changed
deliverable: Replace count comparison with per-test attribution in verdictOf, and carry the meaning into the brief that explains it. TestRun and Baseline both hold only counts today, so the change reaches the parse as well as the verdict. The escalation ladder is where the defect actually bites - a survivor is re-run at whole-suite scope, which is exactly where the known flake fires - so a fix that leaves escalation judging by count has fixed the reproduction and not the property.
evidence: Ruled HIGH by the author 2026-08-06 after the mechanism was read out of the source: scripts/mutate.ts verdictOf is run.failed > wasFailing ? KILLED : SURVIVED, and neither TestRun (failed, passed, total, filesFailed, raw) nor Baseline (failed, total, ran) captures which test failed. Observed live: an auditor re-ran one identical manifest entry against an unchanged tree and got KILLED 2 failed of 1786, then SURVIVED 0 failed of 1786, then a third run reporting one test already failing. Exposure is every mutation verdict in the repository, including every verdict cited in this session's own audits. The flake it rides on is filed separately as npm-test-flakes-on-three-slow-spawn-heavy-tests-under-full-s and is deliberately not this task's job.

title: ma-1: a mutation whose scope holds two failing tests that print the same name gets no verdict at all, where main got the right one
deliverable: Attribution stops depending on printed names being unique, so the whole suite — the scope every escalated survivor lands in — can return a verdict again. parseFailedTests drops the dedupe and tallyOf reconciles multisets (a name printed twice is two failures), or the reconciliation moves to per-file counts, which the run already has in filesFailed. The refusal is then reserved for what it was written for: a reporter this parse genuinely cannot read.
evidence: parseFailedTests dedupes ("if (!named.includes(match[1]))") and tallyOf throws when failures.length < tally.failed. src/content/references.test.ts already contains two it.each blocks whose rendered names collide on the first printed line, because the name's distinguishing part sits after an embedded newline: six rows print as "rejects a result or tag naming nothing:   ability: attack →   ability: attack" and two as "rejects   rate: attack-rate →   rate: attack-rate". Re-runnable: a manifest of file src/content/namespace.ts, find "matches.length === 0", replace "false", tests ["src/content/references.test.ts"]. That line is genuinely watched — 28 of 34 tests go from pass to fail. main (5fec46b) reports "ma-dup  KILLED  28 failed of 34  [src/content/references.test.ts]", 1 killed. This branch reports "0 killed, 0 survived, 0 unstable, 1 errored" with the detail "the run reported 28 failing test(s) and named 22 of them, so no verdict could be attributed to a test". Confirmed against the captured streams directly: parseVitestTally says 28, parseFailedTests says 22, tallyOf throws. This is a regression against main in the tool every audit in the repository depends on, and it lands on the DSL load path's reference-resolution area, which is exactly where a load-path auditor aims.

title: ma-2: the tolerance is asymmetric in the wrong direction, so a run vitest called green can be reported KILLED
deliverable: A name that no counted failure backs cannot carry a verdict. attributed is bounded by run.failed, or the hook-throw case that motivated the tolerance is reconciled explicitly (a FAIL line with no test under it is a suite, and the run already reports filesFailed) instead of by an unbounded allowance. The direction that manufactures proof then costs nothing, which is the asymmetry the comment claims to have.
evidence: The comment at scripts/mutate.ts states "Fewer names than failures is the one direction that costs a verdict". It is not. Nothing anywhere cross-checks attributed against run.failed. tallyOf({ stdout: "      Tests  0 failed | 5 passed (5)", stderr: " FAIL  a.test.ts > s > not actually a failure" }) is accepted, and runMutations over it returns the row "m  KILLED    0 failed of 5  [whole suite]  killed by a.test.ts > s > not actually a failure, re-run at [a.test.ts] with the mutation still applied and failing there too". A verdict of KILLED on zero counted failures is the same defect class this branch exists to remove, reached from the other side: the count and the names are described as independent readings that catch a bad parse by disagreeing, but only one of the two disagreements is checked. No in-repo emitter of a FAIL-shaped line was found on stderr today (scripts/tasks/mergeReady.ts prints FAIL but not at the start of a line), so this is reachability-unproven rather than live — unlike ma-1. The test "accepts more names than failures, which is what a broken hook prints" pins the tolerance without pinning any bound on it, so it is a test agreeing with the implementation's assumption rather than testing it.

title: ma-3: a confirmation run that will not build reads UNSTABLE, which tells the auditor the opposite of what ERROR would
deliverable: The confirmation applies the same run-sanity gate the first measurement does, so "the mutant does not build at this scope" stays an ERROR at both. One condition, one verdict, and the auditor gets one instruction about it.
evidence: verdictOf refuses two shapes before it attributes anything: run.total === 0 ("the run reported no tests — the mutation may not build") and run.filesFailed > 0 && run.failed === 0 ("test file(s) failed to collect — the mutation may not build"). confirmKill checks neither; it looks only at whether the attributed names reappear. Driven through runMutations with injected runTests: a kill found at whole-suite scope whose confirmation run returns { failed: 0, total: 0, filesFailed: 1 } is reported UNSTABLE with detail undefined, and so is one whose confirmation run reports no tests at all. The generated brief tells an auditor UNSTABLE means "this scope cannot answer" and to "say so rather than re-running until it picks a side", while ERROR means "retarget and run it again" — opposite instructions for the identical condition, decided by which of the two functions happened to see it.

title: ma-4: c4 is written unconditionally and holds only for kills, so a survivor is still a coin flip returned as fact
deliverable: Either the promise is narrowed in writing, in the brief and in the usage text, to the direction it actually covers, with the spec's own reasoning as its justification (a false SURVIVED costs an argument, a false KILLED reads as proof); or a survivor at the widest scope it reached is confirmed the same single extra time a kill is. What must not stand is an unqualified clause graded met, because the next pass reads "the same manifest against the same tree reports the same verdicts" and it does not.
evidence: Driven through runMutations with injected runTests over an identical tree and manifest: a run in which the watching test flaked green returns "m  SURVIVED  0 failed of 20  [whole suite]" with no annotation, and a run in which it did not returns KILLED. A verdict changed between identical runs and nothing said why. Only a KILLED enters the confirmation phase ("if (found.verdict !== 'KILLED' || found.attributed === undefined) continue;"). The flaked field covers the opposite crossing only — a test the baseline saw fail and the mutated run saw pass — and is empty here because the baseline was green. The asymmetry is a recorded worker decision, but it is recorded against the task, not in the spec's Decisions, and the clause it qualifies was never amended to say so.

title: ma-5: the confirmation scope is assembled out of the very tests it exists to filter, so it widens with the noise
deliverable: Each attributed test is re-measured at its own file, one vitest invocation per file, rather than the union of them in one. That is the minimum-contention scope, it is what the clause's reasoning implies, and it removes the case where the tool's answer depends on how many flakes happened to fire. It also makes the cost proportional to what is being confirmed rather than to how noisy the wide run was.
evidence: filesOf(found.attributed) returns every file the attributed tests live in, and the confirmation runs them together as one scope. Driven through runMutations with injected runTests: a whole-suite run attributing to a flake in a.test.ts and a flake in b.test.ts produces a confirmation at "a.test.ts, b.test.ts", in which the second reproduces under the two-file contention, and the entry is reported KILLED attributed to that flake. The known flake this branch was written against is contention-driven, so the scope that filters contention growing with the number of contended tests is the wrong direction for it to move. The property survives the ordinary case and this is a residual, not a refutation, which is why c3 is graded met.

title: ma-6: a confirmed row mixes numbers from two different measurements without saying so
deliverable: A confirmed row's numbers come from the run that confirmed it, or the row names the scope each number was measured at. A shortfall warning that belongs to a scope the verdict no longer rests on is a reader being told a true thing about the wrong run.
evidence: confirmKill returns { ...result } and overwrites only verdict, attributed, unreproduced and confirmedAt, so failed, total and shortfall are all carried from the first measurement while the verdict comes from the second. Driven through runMutations: a narrow run with a shortfall whose kill is confirmed at another file formats as "m  KILLED    1 failed of 8  [one.test.ts]  killed by y.test.ts > s > watcher, re-run at [y.test.ts] with the mutation still applied and failing there too  (4 fewer tests ran than the unmutated baseline — they cannot have killed it)". One line asserts a kill and warns that four tests which could not have killed it went missing, and the two statements are about different scopes.

title: ma-7: the usage text still promises that only survivors pay for the wider runs, and a kill now pays most
deliverable: The usage says what a kill costs, beside the sentence that tells a manifest author to name the narrowest scope they can. That advice now buys something different from what it says it buys, and the author choosing a scope is the one person who can act on the difference.
evidence: scripts/mutate.ts usage reads "so only the survivors pay for the wider runs", unchanged, while the confirmation phase added below it charges every kill an extra run. Measured on the same six-entry manifest over the same tree: main (5fec46b) 56s, this branch 97s, +73%, in the cheapest possible case where every entry kills at its own declared file. The narrowest scope the tool offers fares worst in relative terms: an entry naming tests plus a single test confirms at the whole file without the -t filter, so it pays a second baseline at the file scope and a full-file confirmation run — observed live, two baselines measured ("scripts/mutate.test.ts \"kills on a different test failing...\"" then "scripts/mutate.test.ts") for one entry. An escalated whole-suite kill pays a fresh baseline at an ad-hoc multi-file scope plus the confirmation run, both near-suite-width. Nothing here breaches the five-minute rule (npm run tasks -- merge-ready ran the whole gate in 43s) and mutate is not a gate, so this is a documentation and expectation defect rather than a budget one.

title: A named-slot store with a written-at stamp
deliverable: One interface over named slots -- read, write, delete, list -- whose payload is opaque text it never parses, with the instant of the write held beside the payload rather than inside it. A slot reads back byte-identical. The implementation is supplied by the driver: a file under the CLI, in-memory under test, nothing below the driver touching a disk. No load path reads a clock.
evidence: Three queued records asked for slots before this branch was planned: single-dev-mode runs dev work against a separate slot and writes its snapshot to the store rather than holding it in memory (its c1 and c3), offline-progression measures its span from the last slot the store wrote and reasons out why the stamp cannot live in the payload, and save-migration-system wants a real player save to protect. serializeSave's output is the payload verbatim, so an export and a # save fixture are the same bytes. Requires runtime-2026-07-30-h1 because this branch turns a hand-written-fixture-only crash path into one any corrupt slot can reach.

title: A note against an archived record makes the branch owe that record's spec, and no command can unbind it
deliverable: tasks note --id <id> tags its event with the spec of the record it annotates, inherited from that record rather than from the branch. merge-ready's spec source then prefers 'a spec it owes' over 'a plan this branch wrote', so one note against a two-day-old merged clause makes the gate grade this branch against that archived spec. There is no inverse: spec remove unbinds a member, not an event, and the log is append-only by design. Either the ownership inference ignores note and decision events tagged by inheritance, or a branch can state the spec it owes and be believed.
evidence: 2026-08-07 on claude/suite-flake-plan. The branch authored spec a-green-run-means-the-tree-is-green and, following workflow step 10, recorded three notes linking the archive to it. One -- tasks note --id audit-loop-costs-less-clause-5 -- inherited spec audit-loop-costs-less from the clause it annotated. merge-ready then reported 'spec chosen by the gate: audit-loop-costs-less -- a-green-run-means-the-tree-is-green is a plan this branch wrote, and audit-loop-costs-less is a spec it owes', and failed its clauses leg on that spec's c5. Recording a later decision tagged with the correct spec did not displace it: the rule is owed-over-written, not most-recent. Compounded by merge-ready-s-clauses-leg-cannot-see-an-abandoned-clause (open, low): c5 is declined, so the leg reports it outstanding forever and the branch cannot go green by any action. Same shape as the contradiction filed at e3baf17 -- one tool demands what another refuses to produce.
reason: Folded whole into gate-believes-the-branch, which carries it as one of three faults with one root: every spec-standing read routes through decideSpec, the inference ignores a spec tag that reached an event by inheritance, and the clauses leg can see an abandoned clause. Closing it separately would fix the inference in one caller and leave the other two, which is the aimed-at-the-finding failure mode this push is also fixing.

title: a note or title cannot begin with two dashes, because the parser has no end-of-flags separator
deliverable: a positional argument beginning with -- is recordable, by the conventional end-of-flags separator
evidence: Found by U7 while writing a real decision event: tasks decision "--actor is named by each writing command" is parsed as an unknown flag and refused. Pre-existing in U6's arity-aware parser rather than introduced by it — tasks add "--x" has the same shape. The conventional fix is an end-of-flags -- separator, which means touching the parser U7 was told to reuse rather than fork, so it was left alone and the decision reworded. Low: it costs a rephrase, and the refusal is loud rather than silent, which is the polarity c2 asks for.

title: A question's decider changes what the tooling does with it
deliverable: The half of c4 that the record-shape slice could not reach, because it lives outside that slice's grant. Task.decider is stored and displayed and read by nothing: work-prompt on a question addressed to the author prints 'You are implementing <id>' followed by a worker's implementation brief - correct your write grant, register what it produces, commit after each chunk - and start claims it silently. The escalation route loops back to a worker as work to implement, which is the stall c4 exists to prevent wearing a label that says otherwise. State the property and let the mechanism follow: a question reaches its decider, and a question addressed away from the worker is never handed back to one as work. What work-prompt should print for a question addressed to the planner or the author instead of an implementation brief is this task's call, made after reading how cmdWorkPrompt already distinguishes a root record from a member.
evidence: Filed by the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place pass 1 on claude/friction-record as a HIGH, and verified independently before this record was written: filed a question with --decider author against an open member, ran work-prompt on its id, and got the implementation brief verbatim. The clause's own amended text now names this as the property rather than leaving it as a trailing rationale after an enumeration - the ambiguity that let a defensible audit grade the list and miss the point. Second half of a decomposition error made twice: c4 and c6 each span two write regions and each was assigned to one slice, both caught by the agents doing the work rather than by the planner.

title: a record cannot be removed, and a grant cannot be cleared
deliverable: Give the store a route to retract a record that should never have been one, and let tasks edit clear an optional field. Either a delete verb for a declined record nothing references, or accept an empty --grant the way --discharges and --requires already accept one. Both routes exist for other fields; grant is the outlier that refuses the empty value, and there is no route at all for a whole record.
evidence: 2026-08-06: cleaning three scratch probes (scratch-ruling-probe, c11-proof-probe, orch-verify-probe), declined 2026-08-05 as 'not real work', each declaring a forecast grant over an empty writes list so doctor warns on all three. tasks edit --grant '' returns 'must be one of forecast, commitment', and no delete verb exists, so the only route was hand-editing docs/tasks.jsonl -- the one file the system exists to keep agents out of, and the file the-task-store-survives-parallel-branches is about to make sort-canonical.

title: A record cannot leave the store unrecorded
deliverable: EVENT_OPS gains remove, every path that drops a record from the array saveStore writes files one, and a reconciliation returns three disjoint sets over the log and the store while reporting the coverage it does not have. c5 is deliberately excluded from this grant until the author rules on giving doctor a second failure condition; if the ruling is yes it is a separate slice over doctor.ts. The four live discrepancies are adjudicated in the store as part of c6, not left as the check's first output.
evidence: Planned in another session, verified against the tree before adoption rather than taken on report: the four orphaned ids resolve exactly as claimed, proof-targets-resolve returns nothing from git log --all -S over docs/tasks.jsonl on every reachable ref, EVENT_OPS holds sixteen verbs and spec-remove is about spec membership rather than store presence. One number corrected: 160 store records carry an add event, not 164. REQUIRES the recurrence slice rather than running beside it, and the reason is measured today: both add to EVENT_OPS, which is a single array literal, and two branches appending at one array position is the same shared-append-point shape that conflicted in docs/audits/systems.json on this session's own trial merge. File-level overlap is not merge-level overlap, but a shared append point is.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 5: **`doctor` keeps exactly one failure condition.** An unexplained absence is named, counted and printed on every run that finds one, and changes no exit code. Ruled by the author 2026-08-06, refusing this clause's original form: one historical absence is the case for reporting it, not for failing the build on the store's own history. `doctor-fix` cannot repair it either — a record the store lost is not a record `doctor` may invent, so the action is to file the ruling, not to write the row back. Written as a refusal rather than deleted, because a deleted clause leaves the gate available to the next branch that finds the argument locally reasonable, and this exact gate was proposed twice in one day from two independent directions.
deliverable: **`doctor` keeps exactly one failure condition.** An unexplained absence is named, counted and printed on every run that finds one, and changes no exit code. Ruled by the author 2026-08-06, refusing this clause's original form: one historical absence is the case for reporting it, not for failing the build on the store's own history. `doctor-fix` cannot repair it either — a record the store lost is not a record `doctor` may invent, so the action is to file the ruling, not to write the row back. Written as a refusal rather than deleted, because a deleted clause leaves the gate available to the next branch that finds the argument locally reasonable, and this exact gate was proposed twice in one day from two independent directions.
evidence: The reconciliation half of this clause is proven and I want that on the record: an unexplained absence is named and counted at doctor.ts:79-80, changes no exit code, and `--fix` does not repair it. Mutations, both KILLED and re-confirmed at doctor.test.ts: deleting the `printReconciliation(config, tasks);` call killed by "names an unexplained absence, counts it, and still exits zero"; and the negative-direction mutation — making the absence a gate while printing byte-identical lines, `for (const id of absentUnexplained) if ((process.exitCode = 1)) console.log(...)` — was also KILLED by that test, so the suite does watch the exit code and not just the text. What fails is the clause's headline. At the merge base the comment read "The only condition that exits non-zero" (`git show 9f5f4dd:scripts/tasks/doctor.ts`); at HEAD scripts/tasks/doctor.ts:121 reads "The two conditions that exit non-zero" and doctor exits 1 on `dangling > 0` as well, added inside this same diff range by f2b0383 for c9 of a-silent-answer-is-a-defect. Reproduced live: the sandbox run at C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass1-e1.sh ends "0 unparseable line(s)" and "doctor exit=1". CLAUDE.md line 47 still reads "`doctor` fails on one condition only: a `docs/tasks.jsonl` line that will not parse", so the branch merges the one document every agent reads as ground truth stating a false gate contract, and this clause — written as a standing refusal precisely so the gate could not be re-argued — restates the false count. Recorded unmet rather than met-with-a-note because a met verdict would put that sentence in the store as verified. The fix is small and is filed as a finding: name both conditions in CLAUDE.md, and restate c5 as what it actually forbids.

title: c2's closure is asserted rather than enforced: `saveStore`'s `removing` parameter lets a caller declare a drop and write no event, and nothing fails when a second caller appears
deliverable: The declaration and the event come from one place — either saveStore appends the remove events itself, which the layering permits since eventLog.ts and taskStore.ts are both scripts/lib, or a test fails when scripts/ gains a second `saveStore(` call site. Then "an op added later cannot re-open the hole by being write-path-only" is a property the suite holds rather than a claim about today's call graph, which is the durable half the spec says it is buying.
evidence: c2 is true today because saveStore has exactly one non-test caller (grep over scripts/ for `saveStore(` outside *.test.ts: the definition at taskStore.ts:613 and context.ts:205), and the pairing that writes the event lives in that caller. `saveStore(tasks, path, ['x'])` from any new call site passes the undeclared-drop guard and appends nothing, and no test in the tree fails for it — I checked by looking for the pattern the repository already uses for this shape: scripts/tasks/friction.test.ts:716 pins a source-level invariant by reading its own module and asserting a regex over it, and the spec's own Deliverable cites `every-triage-action-has-a-non-interactive-form`'s completeness table as the model. Neither was applied here, so the set is closed by convention across a module boundary.

title: CLAUDE.md and c5 both state `doctor` has exactly one failure condition; this branch ships two and changes neither sentence
deliverable: CLAUDE.md line 47 names both conditions, and c5 is restated as the refusal it actually is — the reconciliation adds no failure condition — so the document every agent reads as ground truth is not false about the one gate the repository has, and a clause written to stop a gate being re-argued does not carry a count that the next reader can disprove in one command.
evidence: At the merge base doctor had one exit: `git show 9f5f4dd:scripts/tasks/doctor.ts` ends "the only condition doctor fails on". At HEAD, doctor.ts:121 reads "The two conditions that exit non-zero" and lines 128-136 exit 1 on unparseable lines and on `dangling > 0`, the second added by f2b0383 inside this range. CLAUDE.md:47 is unchanged and still reads "`doctor` fails on one condition only: a `docs/tasks.jsonl` line that will not parse", and the diff over the range touches no CLAUDE.md. Live: the sandbox doctor run prints "0 unparseable line(s)" and exits 1. c5's own body argues that a refusal must stay written down "because a deleted clause leaves the gate available to the next branch that finds the argument locally reasonable, and this exact gate was proposed twice in one day" — and the next phase of this same branch added a gate to doctor from a third direction, which is the case for repairing the sentence rather than leaving two documents disagreeing.

title: `reconcile` reads the last explaining event regardless of whether the record was created again after it, so a re-filed record that vanishes again reads as accounted for
deliverable: An explanation counts only when it is the last `remove` or `decline` after that id's last `add`, so a record that came back and then went missing lands in the finding set instead of under a stale reason — which is what makes "the third set is the finding" true rather than nearly true. The test that covers the line changes shape too: the current case cannot fail on the property, so it needs the add-after-remove ordering, not another add,remove,add,remove.
evidence: `events.filter((event) => event.id === id && EXPLAINS_ABSENCE.includes(event.op)).pop()` ignores position relative to `add`. Via `npm run inspect`: reconcile([add 'twice', remove 'twice' 'first time, on purpose', add 'twice'], []) returns absentExplained [{id:'twice',op:'remove',note:'first time, on purpose'}] and absentUnexplained [], and reconcile([add 'x', decline 'x' 'not real work', triage 'x' 'retriaged', start 'x' 'claimed', edit 'x'], []) returns absentExplained [{id:'x',op:'decline',note:'not real work'}]. Both are records the log says were live after the explanation and are now gone — the deliberately-dropped versus silently-gone distinction this branch buys, reported the wrong way round. The existing test "reads the last explanation, so a record removed and then re-created and removed again reads as removed" is add,remove,add,remove, where both rules give the same answer, so it cannot distinguish them; retriage after a decline and re-filing under the same id are both ordinary operations here.

title: `tasks remove` checks no precondition, so the one route out of the store manufactures the state `doctor` now exits non-zero on
deliverable: cmdRemove names, before it writes, everything the removal is about to break — every record whose `requires` holds the id, and any live claim on the record it is deleting — and either refuses or releases the holds the way `cmdDone` already does at records.ts:1041-1046. Then the one route a record may leave the store by cannot leave the store failing the merge gate, and the removal verb acquires the same precondition discipline every other write verb in the file has.
evidence: Reproduced in an isolated store (script kept at C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass1-e1.sh): three records where `blocked` requires `goner`; `tasks remove goner --reason "scratch probe"` exits 0 and prints "the record is gone and the log says so, with the reason"; the next `tasks doctor` prints "[dangling] blocked requires unresolved id: goner", "1 dangling reference(s)" and exits 1. Nothing in cmdRemove looks at `requires` — the whole body is records.ts:353-395 — while `dangling > 0` became a failure condition inside this same diff range (f2b0383), so the two halves of one branch collide: c1/c2 add a verb that produces exactly the state c9 rejects, and the failure surfaces on the next doctor or merge-ready run rather than at the write. The same command also deletes an in-progress record claimed by another actor without mentioning the claim: `add held; start held --actor worker-a; remove held --reason "not wanted" --actor worker-b` leaves an empty store and exits 0, where `tasks start` refuses to take another actor's claim. Both are the same missing check, which is why the deliverable is a precondition and not a special case for `requires`.

title: The reconciliation states its coverage of the store and nothing about its coverage of the log, so one unreadable log line makes an unexplained absence vanish silently
deliverable: printReconciliation reports the log lines it could not read beside the store records it could not check — the number is already in hand, since loadEvents returns `.skipped` and doctor.ts:78 destructures past it — so a run that has gone blind is distinguishable from a clean one. That is c4's own rule ("state your coverage or do not ship") applied to the second input, and without it the branch's deliverable fails open on exactly the input it is a reader of.
evidence: Reproduced end to end (script kept at C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass1-e4.sh). In an isolated store, add `vanished`, delete its row by hand, and `tasks doctor` prints "1 record(s) absent with nothing explaining it" and "[absent] vanished". Truncate the id field of that record's `add` line in events.jsonl and the identical store prints "0 record(s) absent with nothing explaining it, 0 absent and accounted for", no [absent] line, "0 unparseable line(s)" (that count is the store's), and exits 0. So the one signal this branch exists to produce is erased by a single malformed log line with nothing said. The log is append-only and hand-edited during merges, so a bad line is not hypothetical; the store side already carries a coverage number for the same reason, and the log side carries none.

title: The `store removal record` concept's paths omit the two files implementing the half its own note describes
deliverable: The concept covers scripts/tasks/records.ts and scripts/tasks/context.ts alongside the two lib files, so `tasks where scripts/tasks/records.ts` and `tasks produces "store removal record"` answer from the files that implement the capability — which is the whole point of the query an agent runs before building something that exists.
evidence: 11ca3f3 registers the concept over scripts/lib/eventLog.ts and scripts/lib/taskStore.ts while its note reads "the remove op and tasks remove, saveStore refusing an undeclared drop, and reconcile ...". `tasks remove` is cmdRemove at scripts/tasks/records.ts:353 and the Removal/event pairing that makes the declaration inseparable from the event is scripts/tasks/context.ts:196-215; neither file is covered, so neither surfaces the concept. The sibling concept `friction recurrence` in the same manifest does cover its command file (scripts/tasks/records.ts) beside scripts/lib/eventLog.ts, so the convention exists and this registration departs from it.

title: A whitespace-only reason is accepted, so an absence with no stated cause is still recordable and reads as accounted for
deliverable:
Both guards test the trimmed reason rather than its truthiness, in one place both
  verbs read, so `remove` and `decline` agree and neither can file a blank cause. That is the state
  c1's own sentence says this branch exists to make impossible, and the check belongs where the
  reason is assembled rather than duplicated at two call sites.
evidence:
Measured, in an isolated store, by
  C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass2-p1.sh:
  `tasks remove ws-probe --reason "   "` exits 0, prints "the record is gone and the log says so,
  with the reason", and appends {"op":"remove","id":"ws-probe", ... ,"note":"removed from the store:
  "} with three spaces where the cause goes. The following `tasks doctor` then reports "1 absent and
  accounted for" — the branch's own reader counting a blank cause as an explanation, which is what
  c1 calls "the exact state this branch exists to make impossible". The guard is falsy-only at
  records.ts:347 and cmdDecline is identical at records.ts:1123, so the clause's "on the same ground
  `decline` refuses one" is accurate and both verbs share the hole; that is why this is filed rather
  than graded against c1. `--reason ""` is refused, which is the case the existing test covers.

title: c2's closure is asserted by a file-identity text scan, and a second call site inside context.ts survives all 2056 tests
deliverable:
The assertion is about the number of call sites rather than the set of files that
  contain one, or better, the pairing stops being a scan at all: give `saveStore` a required
  argument that writes the removal events, so a caller that declares a drop cannot omit the event by
  construction. CLAUDE.md's own line is the rule here, enforce where the value is assembled rather
  than where it is written, and 28a3a6e's commit message argues against exactly the shape it then
  used for the third time in one commit.
evidence:
taskStore.test.ts:1231-1235 collects the non-test files under scripts/ whose text matches
  /\bsaveStore\s*\(/ and asserts the list equals ['scripts/tasks/context.ts'], and 28a3a6e's message
  claims "a second `saveStore(` anywhere under `scripts/` reddens". Measured against that claim, and
  it is false in two reachable directions. First, aimed and run: the manifest entry "c2 a second
  saveStore call site appears inside context.ts itself" adds a second call site to context.ts and
  SURVIVED, scope walking the named test then the file then the whole suite, 0 failed of 2056 — the
  file is already in the expected list, so its contents are never counted. Second, from the regex
  itself: `import { saveStore as writeStore }` in a new file calls the function through a name the
  scan cannot see, and a scan over the import instead of the call has the same problem the other
  way. What the runtime still refuses is narrower and worth saying, because it bounds the severity:
  an *undeclared* drop from any second caller is still refused by saveStore itself, so the reachable
  hole is a second caller that declares the drop and writes no event, which is what pass 1's finding
  said and what this test was written to close.

title: `remove`'s refusal is justified by a uniqueness claim that `tasks edit --requires` falsifies at exit 0
deliverable:
The comment states the boundary it actually draws rather than a uniqueness it does not
  have: a removal refuses because dropping the edge is the holder's decision, while a forward
  requirement is deliberate and is reported. Either that, or the existing report-and-warn pattern
  ten lines away in the same file is reused for the removal too, which is what a repository with one
  policy for one state looks like. A stated boundary with reasoning is worth more than a false
  superlative, and the same edit closes the "one store condition" copy in the stderr beside it.
evidence:
records.ts:378 reads "this is the one write that can manufacture the state `doctor` exits
  non-zero on". Measured false: in
  C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass2-p3.sh,
  `tasks edit real-work --requires ghost` exits 0, prints "recorded 1 requirement(s) no record
  answers to: ghost" from records.ts:73, and the next `tasks doctor` prints "[dangling] real-work
  requires unresolved id: ghost" and exits 1 over a store with no unparseable line. So the tree
  already sanctions a write that manufactures the exact state, reports it, and stays at exit 0,
  which is the policy `remove` departs from without saying that it is departing. The refusal itself
  is sound and I am not asking for it back: `requires` is the only Task field that holds a record id
  (checked against the interface at scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:25-95 and against every `dangling`
  issue at taskStore.ts:988-1017, where the other three are a duplicate id, a system name and a spec
  file, none of which a removal can strand), and both directions of the guard are mutation-KILLED,
  the over-strict direction by records.test.ts > "removes a record nothing requires once the edge is
  dropped where it belongs". It is the sentence that is wrong, not the code.

title: The one-condition census pass 1 filed survives in three more places, one of them user-facing stderr written by this round's own fix
deliverable:
No place in the tree states that `doctor` has one failure condition. doctor.ts:68's

Pass 1's finding named CLAUDE.md:47 and scripts/tasks/doctor.ts:121. ea752e3 changed

  measured: the sandbox at
  C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass2-p3.sh
  ends "doctor exit=1" on a dangling reference over a store with 0 unparseable lines. The Decision

title: The reconciliation's explanation rule reads file order, and the event log is merge=union, so it is not time order
deliverable:
lastExplanation decides on the events' own `t` rather than on their position in the
  file, which every event already carries and renderEvent already writes first — sort the id's own
  events by `t` before the backward scan, or compare timestamps instead of indices. The regression
  format is one more case in eventLog.test.ts alongside the add/remove/add one: the same three events
  shuffled into union order must give the same verdict, which is the assertion the current test
  cannot make because it never varies the order.
evidence:
65ac499 replaced "the last explanation anywhere" with "the last explanation after the id's
  last add", scanning `own` backwards by index at eventLog.ts:203-206. `own` is file order:
  parseEvents preserves line order and nothing sorts. `.gitattributes` sets `docs/events.jsonl
  merge=union`, which keeps both sides of a conflicting tail hunk and orders them by side rather than
  by clock, so two branches appending events land out of time order. Reproduced through the real
  function, not by reading it: `npm run inspect -- -` over
  C:\Users\yonat\AppData\Local\Temp\audit-a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded-pass2-p2.js
  gives {'time order [add,remove,add]': {explained: [], unexplained: ['x']}, 'union order
  [add,add,remove]': {explained: [{id:'x',op:'remove'}], unexplained: []}} — the same three events,
  opposite verdicts, and the union order returns exactly the wrong one pass 1 filed. Not
  hypothetical: over docs/events.jsonl at this head, 20 adjacent line pairs are out of `t` order and
  3 ids have their own events out of order (spec-done-writes-no-event,
  merge-ready-s-clauses-leg-cannot-see-an-abandoned-clause, run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel
  -tasks). None of the three currently inverts an add against an explanation, so the branch's answer
  today is right; the rule it is right by is not.

title: The `store removal record` concept still omits doctor.ts, where the coverage statement its own note describes actually lives
deliverable:
The concept's paths cover every file implementing it, which is the property pass 1's
  finding was an instance of rather than its whole extent: add scripts/tasks/doctor.ts, where
  printReconciliation is the run-on-every-run coverage statement c4 and c5 are entirely about.
evidence:
The concept's note says it covers "reconcile over the log against the store with the
  coverage it does not have". reconcile computes it; scripts/tasks/doctor.ts:77-86 is the only place
  it is stated on every run, and it is where both of the clauses that mention coverage are
  discharged. ea752e3 added exactly the two files pass 1 named, context.ts and records.ts, and
  stopped there. Reading systems.json at this head, no concept of any system claims
  scripts/tasks/doctor.ts, so this is not a two-concepts-claim-one-file collision but an omission:
  `npm run tasks -- merge-ready`'s audit-status leg lists ten doubly-claimed paths and doctor.ts is
  not among them.

title: A record carries its fault, and a question blocks only what depends on it
deliverable: The channel's data shape and every write route that can create one. Fault becomes a required field on the record, validated where the record is assembled rather than where a reader looks for it, on every route that can produce one - which is the repository's own recorded wisdom and the thing both of the orchestrated run's audit findings turned on. Blocking is deliberately NOT a field: it stays derived from requires and isBlocked, and this task's job on c3 is to prove the refusal holds rather than to build something. The question kind comes alive - it is declared in Kind, present in KINDS, accepted by tasks add, and used by zero records - as the route by which an agent files a design question that halts exactly what depends on it and nothing else.
evidence: The remedy for run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks c3, which is deferred out of that spec still unmet and is the acceptance test for c4 here. That clause failed because the orchestrator at 17:57:22Z had a worker blocked on a design question and only two options, rule or stall, and any orchestrator takes the first. Nothing new is needed for the halt: isBlocked is waitingOn().length > 0 and requirementStates releases on both done and declined.

title: A recorded audit pass is never checked against the diff being merged
deliverable: check --merge refuses when the latest pass head is not an ancestor of HEAD, naming how many commits have landed since the audit.
evidence: cmdAudit computes base and head from git specifically to pin the reviewed range; checkMergeGate reads only verdicts and pass number. Audit once, then land any amount of unaudited code, and the gate stays green. Rule 2 says the audit reads a diff; nothing verifies which diff.

title: A recurrence is appended, and filing shows what already claims the path
deliverable: The write half of recurrence, and the prompt that makes it reachable. Recording that a friction happened again appends an occurrence carrying its own note and naming the record it recurs on. Nothing is incremented anywhere: a counter is a field concurrent branches edit by construction, and .gitattributes states that exact case as why the store is not merge=union, while docs/events.jsonl IS union for the stated reason that two branches appending is always resolvable by keeping both. The derivation of the count belongs to the query slice and c10 names both owners. Second half: filing a record prints what already claims the path it names, by path and never by title, and NEVER REFUSES - priorArt already reads every record's writes and files in every state with containment both ways, so this is wiring an existing query into an existing command rather than a new capability. Attaching an occurrence is available and deliberate; filing new stays the cheap default, because a duplicate is visible and cheap to triage while a wrong merge makes a distinct defect vanish and the count lie.
evidence: Author's proposal 2026-08-06, ruled the same day: the goal adopted whole, the mechanism changed from a stored counter to an appended occurrence for the merge reason above, and the check ruled prompt-never-refuse rather than a refusal or an auto-attach. The measurement that motivates it is the branch's own: the mutation-manifest friction recurred at least nine times across one 3.5-hour run and ranked below a friction hit exactly once, because prose does not aggregate and nothing counted. Its nine instances also differed by spec, by pass and by what each cost, which is why an appended occurrence keeping its own note is not the same as one description overwritten nine times - the author's store-does-not-grow requirement is met either way, and only one of them keeps the variation that shows the shape.

title: A shape change stamped writtenFor: SAVE_VERSION rather than a literal defeats the staleness check silently
deliverable: Either the declaration stops being able to name SAVE_VERSION — e.g. migrate takes the version it is bumping to from an argument and compares it to a literal the declaration carries — or the check gains something that can tell a literal from a reference. Nothing today distinguishes them, and the difference is the whole mechanism.
evidence: Introduced by the fix for save-fixture-migration-pass1-a-stale-shape-change-from-the-p. ShapeChange.writtenFor is compared to SAVE_VERSION, so a declaration written as { writtenFor: SAVE_VERSION, ... } is perpetually current and can never go stale — which is exactly the hole that made NO_FIELD_MOVED unable to survive as a constant and forced noFieldMoved(version). The refusal message asks for a literal, and the test suite has no way to notice if a bump's author does not oblige. Low because the failure needs an author to write the wrong thing after being told, and the message tells them at the moment they need it.
reason: Folded into the task migrate-saves-guards-cannot-be-defeated-by-writing-the-decla, which carries both halves and the low that is the first half's own residual. One seam, one record; the evidence for each is quoted there. Human triage 2026-08-07: deferred rather than fixed on this branch because the tool ships SHAPE_CHANGE = null and refuses by default, so neither hole opens until a bump author writes a declaration.
trigger: the first SAVE_VERSION bump that declares a shape change

title: A lock left behind by a killed write refuses every store write for up to 30 seconds and blames a holder that does not exist
deliverable:
Make the wait outlast the abandonment threshold, or break a lock whose recorded pid is not
 running — the lock file already holds the pid and nothing reads it. And say "was left behind by a write
 that did not finish" when the lock is stale, rather than "is held by another write", which sends the
 reader looking for a process that is not there.
evidence:
LOCK_WAIT_MS is 5s and LOCK_ABANDONED_MS is 30s, so the abandonment break can only fire for a
 writer that happens to arrive more than 30s after the kill; every writer arriving before then spends the
 full 5s spinning and refuses. Measured: with a `<store>.lock` present and no holder, saveStore refused
 after 5021ms with `… is held by another write and did not clear within 5000ms. Nothing was written;
 re-run the command.` The same lock back-dated past 30s was broken and the write landed in 13ms. The
 .gitignore comment added by this branch says a leftover lock is broken automatically after 30s, which is
 true of the lock and not of the 30 seconds of writes that fail first.

title: A record closed without ever being started accepts --grant commitment
deliverable:
Gate on the record having actually been taken — in-progress, or closed with a recorded actor
 or start event — rather than on the state being non-open. The field's whole job is to say someone read
 the region, and it is the input to the grant-versus-diff measurement c7 introduces, so a commitment
 asserted after the fact falsifies the only measurement anyone has of how wrong a forecast is.
evidence:
claimHolds admits CLOSING_STATES, and a record reaches `done` from `open` without `tasks start`.
 Reproduced through the real CLI: `tasks add w --id w1 --writes src/runtime/` then `tasks done w1` (exit 0,
 "was open") then `tasks edit w1 --grant commitment` exits 0 and prints `edited w1: grant`. The same edit
 against the same record while it was open exits 1 with "records that someone has read the region". Same
 result for a declined record. The clause says the word is refused on a record nobody has started, and w1
 is a record nobody started.

title: c10's declared proof target does not hold c10
deliverable:
Point c10's proof at scripts/tasks/doctor.test.ts, or add the checkStore case to
 taskStore.test.ts — one assertion that a closed record naming a missing spec produces no issue, beside
 the existing "flags a spec with no file" which uses the default open state. Either makes the clause's
 stated proof a thing a next pass can re-run; today re-running it proves nothing.
evidence:
The clause declares `proof: vitest scripts/lib/taskStore.test.ts`. That file's checkStore block
 has an assertion for an open record with a missing spec and none for a closed one, so nothing in it can
 fail on the CLOSING_STATES guard the clause is about. Measured rather than read: I ran the mutation that
 removes `!CLOSING_STATES.includes(task.state) &&` from scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:939 with the scope set to
 scripts/lib/taskStore.test.ts alone. It survived there, escalated to the whole suite, and was killed by
