title: An item is a hex plane grown by slotting cluster jewels
evidence: Spec rewritten 2026-08-07, DSL and content settled against the real grammar and the real stat fold in docs/smithing/cluster-jewels-draft.dsl (28 passives, 11 cluster jewels, 4 orbs). Topology is a closed hard-coded shape catalogue in src/content, deleting the topology grammar and replacing per-jewel reachability with one test over the catalogue. A '# cluster-jewel' names a shape, lists open-connections (1-5 of the five non-root edges), declares mod-slots (default 2) and fills numbered positions with '# passive' references; an unfilled position is a real node that costs a point and grants nothing. A passive's payload may not be a range, so nothing is stored per position. CLUSTER EFFECTS: four orbs declaring 'cluster-effect: +25% <stat>', applied to a cluster already standing in a plane rather than to a jewel in inventory, which keeps jewels stackable and uninstanced. An effect scales every payload naming its stat in that cluster only, in whichever channel it lands - a +10 becomes +12.5 and a +10% becomes +12.5%. Effects on one cluster POOL ADDITIVELY, exactly as fold.increased already does in statRange: two 25% effects are 50%, not 56.25%. The compounding a player feels comes from the fold multiplying the two scaled channels, not from effects multiplying each other; the mechanic is multiplicative in result and additive in composition. Pinned worked case against the real fold (max-health base 30, a +10 and a +10% allocated): 44 unmodified, 47.8125 with one effect, 51.75 with two - and 51.75 is 51.74999999999999 in float, so the test needs a tolerance. 'more' is the reserved word if a truly multiplicative modifier is ever wanted. Clause-tagged c1-c23.

title: Give merge-ready this branch's standing and stop its summary swallowing doctor's warnings

evidence: Found on claude/gui-rebuild-specs-1feb26 on 2026-08-07, the same shape as planning-branch-friction. That branch retired graph-based-items-research by declining its only member, because the design it gated was replaced. merge-ready then fails its clauses leg: 'graph-based-items-research has no recorded audit pass'. But audit-prompt for that same spec prints a WARNING that the branch is working archetype-mods, that the clauses would be graded against a diff that does not contain their implementation, and step 7 reads 'Do not file a pass ... which is why no pass file was written'. The two tools contradict each other: one demands an artifact the other refuses to produce, and there is no action a branch can take to go green. The rule gap is planning-branch-friction c1, which treats any member that is not open as work done here: 'A member that is in-progress, done or declined is work done here and the branch owes the spec exactly as it did before.' Right for done and in-progress, wrong for declined. Declining every member of a spec is a RETRACTION, not work against its clauses - there is no implementation to audit and never will be, which is what audit-prompt already detects and says. Candidate rule: a spec whose members are all closed and none done is retired, and owes no clause. Deliberately narrow - one done member means real work happened and the spec is owed as before. Prior art on this inference: spec-and-read-verbs-scope (done), no-store-inference-on-main (done), a-branch-knows-which-spec-it-owes (done, the third pass, holds the write commitment on mergeReady.ts). This is the fourth case, and unlike the first three the failure is a contradiction between two tools rather than a wrong answer from one.

title: Merge-ready runs its independent legs together

evidence: Outcome of the audit-prompt-drift-and-isolation discussion, decided 2026-08-06. merge-ready already runs npm test, so the wall and the per-file durations are free; audit-prompt would need its own run or stale numbers, and drift is a repo property rather than a branch one. The test leg gains one line: the wall, and the slowest file with its duration. It warns above 45s and never fails on time -- merge-ready is not in CI (CI runs tsc, npm test, layer-check, audit-status, doctor, spec show and plan), so the threshold only ever runs on a developer's machine and is portable enough to mean something. Baseline at decision time: 28.9s wall, 175.5s summed over 69 files, slowest scripts/tasks/audit.test.ts at 27.2s. title: The batch-of-one fallback walks one segment per completion for as long as the pool stays non-empty, and the commit's performance claim understates its worst shape

evidence:
Measured with npm run inspect over a 4h span (14400s), a repeating 1s action draining a 30-unit on-empty

title: One query over the channel, and the second place retired
deliverable: The read half, and the deletion that makes it the only half. One query reports the channel grouped by fault, the breaches per lesson, and every count beside the denominator it is a rate over - drawn from events the log already carries (start for dispatches, since a work-prompt is a read and leaves no event; audit for passes; spec-done for specs closed) rather than from a tally anyone maintains by hand. Fault nobody is REPORTED and never COUNTED as a defect: the two are different acts and c5 turns on the difference. A lesson checked and found clean is distinguishable from one nobody looked at. audit.ts step 8 stops instructing auditors to write prose into a tracked markdown file and files into the channel instead, docs/workflow.md follows, and .planning/agent-feedback/tool-friction.md is deleted. Nothing gates: c9 is a refusal proven by test, not a feature.
evidence: The measurement that justifies the whole branch is inside the file this task deletes. The mutation manifest that never generates - proof: vitest <file> names a file where mutationManifest needs a test - appears in eight separate pass entries at about ten minutes each across the 2026-08-06 run and has no record, while audit-prompt's wrong WARNING, hit exactly once, is filed high and will be fixed. Prose does not aggregate, so the friction that recurs is exactly the friction that stays invisible. The file is retired rather than migrated: it is treated the way a merged spec is treated, history once its lessons are extracted, and rewriting 866 lines of pass narrative into structured records would be a third copy of everything. Its recurring frictions are filed as records by this branch's planning instead. Git holds every word.

title: One writer for the mod portal's enabled intent

The only code that persists enabled intent is toggle() inside scripts/modportal.ts, which mutates manifest.intent and writes the file itself. Continuing past a failed save load has to persist a disable, and doing that from play-cli would make a second writer of one manifest. The seam is added beside the read seam and toggle is moved onto it. Reuses the mod portal capability the Contribution system already owns rather than declaring a second one.

title: ORCHESTRATOR_LESSONS instruction 1 tells an orchestrator to route every decision it could make itself, which the decision-placement reframe contradicts
deliverable: The instruction reads 'Route a design question you could answer yourself to a planning session anyway - not to move it off the author's desk, but to move it where the survey and the rulings already are.' That is a blanket prohibition, and it is now known to be the wrong shape. The rule the author settled is placement: route a decision to whoever decides it most durably, which is sometimes the orchestrator and is very often the worker that has just read the code. As written the instruction generates the failure it is trying to prevent, since an orchestrator following it either escalates a mechanical call that the worker should own, or ignores the instruction and rules anyway, which is what the observed run did. Rewrite as a placement test with the durability criterion, not as a prohibition. It also carries a second problem worth fixing in the same edit: it gives escalation no destination, and a question with no decider is a stall.
evidence: Decision recorded 2026-08-06 against the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place: a decision made in the wrong place gets re-decided, and the re-decision is the cost. run-an-orchestrator's own log supplies three instances, all of them the orchestrator deciding mid-run rather than in planning, and all of them re-decided later: the 18:42:16Z re-ruling of pass 1's spec-ownership threshold, the 16:00:12Z correction that named a dead-code site, and the fix-the-neighbour pattern three for three. The lesson is shipped in the generated orchestrator brief and its literal text is asserted by orchestratePrompt.test.ts, so changing it changes a test. Filed rather than fixed because briefLessons.ts is the grant of a-lesson-has-a-handle-that-survives-rewording-it, whose job is handles and not content, and folding a content rewrite into it would conflate two changes in one file.
reason: Folded whole into lessons-say-what-the-run-learned. All three are content in the brief lesson tables, all three were filed rather than fixed because briefLessons.ts was another task's grant, and that task -- a-lesson-has-a-handle-that-survives-rewording-it -- merges immediately before this one. Fixing them in three branches would mean three rewrites of one file for changes that share a reviewer's single reading. The orchestrator-records finding contributes only its free half, the rule that a worker never cites an id it cannot resolve; where an orchestrator files during a parallel run stays open as a planning question for whenever the freeze lifts, since no parallel run happens during it.

title: Ordering another spec's member makes this branch declare that spec, and owe its clauses
deliverable: The declared-spec derivation distinguishes a branch that worked a spec's member from one that only re-pointed it. A --requires edge, a --system correction or a triage move changes a record without touching the work the spec promises, and the branch that made it should not be graded on clauses it never touched.
evidence: Reproduced on claude/task-system-audit-impl-09cdb4 at e278610. The branch's only interaction with a-lesson-is-folded-from-its-own-log was 'tasks edit ... --requires lessons-say-what-the-run-learned', the ordering the 2026-08-08 sweep section 7.4 asked for as a ruling. merge-ready then reports 'spec a-lesson-is-folded-from-its-own-log FAIL 1 open member(s)' and 'clauses ... FAIL ... has no recorded audit pass', so obeying the sweep's instruction to rule on a collision before dispatch is what makes the ruling branch unmergeable. docs/workflow.md:86 states the rule it follows: every task record that changed between the merge base and this checkout, filtered to the ones naming a spec.

title: parseFailedTests must keep every printed FAIL line, and one test now pins only the distinct case
deliverable: The dedupe is removed and the correspondence with the tally is restored, but nothing in mutate.test.ts fails if it is put back: no test feeds parseFailedTests two identical FAIL lines and asserts both survive. The property is that the parse reports what vitest PRINTED, not a distinct set of it, because tallyOf refuses a run whose names are fewer than its tally and a collapsed name reads as a reporter it could not parse. Add the test that would have caught the original, and while there consider whether attributed should be de-duplicated at the point it is REPORTED rather than at the point it is parsed - the two are different questions and only one of them is the guard's.
evidence: Filed by the orchestrator 2026-08-07 alongside the fix, because the fix landed after this branch's pass 1 was recorded and is therefore unaudited. Reproduced before and after: mutating src/content/namespace.ts:97 (matches.length === 0 -> false) and running src/content/references.test.ts yields 28 failing tests and 22 distinct printed FAIL names, because six it.each rows print one identical name and two print another - their distinguishing part follows an embedded newline. Before the fix tallyOf threw and the entry read ERROR where main reported KILLED 28 failed of 34; after it, parseFailedTests returns 28 names of which 22 are distinct and the guard passes. mutate.test.ts is 149 passing either way, which is the gap this finding names.

title: merge-ready reports "every leg passed" on a planning branch whose own spec was never audited
deliverable: A planning branch is exactly the shape the spec describes: it ships a deliverable under its own spec and then writes a spec for a later branch. `merge-ready` grades one spec, whichever `resolveActiveSpec` picked, and on a worktree branch (`claude/<topic>-<hash>`, this repo's convention) the branch-name route misses and the event-log route picks the most recently written spec — the plan, because planning happens last. `specAuthoredHere` then turns that spec's two red legs green and drops the clauses leg entirely, so the gate says "merge-ready: every leg passed / then merge <branch> into main" while the spec the branch actually delivered is never mentioned and its clauses are never graded. Before this branch the same misresolution produced a red gate, which is loud and wrong; it is now green and wrong, and the false green is on the one gate that certifies a branch. Fixing it means merge-ready either grading every spec this branch touched, or naming the spec it resolved and how (`resolveActiveSpec` already returns that note and merge-ready discards it) so a reader can see it graded the wrong one.
evidence:
Reproduced end to end with a fixture in a temp dir. Store built with `npm run tasks -- add ... --store <tmp>/tasks.jsonl --specs-dir <tmp>/specs --branch claude/topic-abc`: spec real-work with member real-slice taken to done (a real deliverable), then spec plan-for-later with members plan-a and plan-b left open (the plan). Both spec files written into <tmp>/specs; neither has an audit pass.
`npm run tasks -- next --store <tmp>/tasks.jsonl --specs-dir <tmp>/specs --branch claude/topic-abc` prints `spec inferred from the event log: plan-for-later - the most recent spec written from claude/topic-abc`, so the plan shadows the delivered spec (context.ts:236, lastSpecWrittenFromBranch).
`npm run tasks -- merge-ready --store <tmp>/tasks.jsonl --specs-dir <tmp>/specs --branch claude/topic-abc` then prints `spec  ok  pass - this branch wrote plan-for-later as a plan for a later branch and worked none of its 2 member(s), so it owes neither them nor a clause`, no clauses leg, `merge-ready: every leg passed`, `then merge claude/topic-abc into main`. real-work is never named and its clause is never graded.
On the base commit the same fixture is red on both legs by inspection of the diff: without the mergeReady.ts:103 early return, `openMembers` is [plan-a, plan-b] so the spec leg fails, and `auditPasses` is 0 so the clauses leg fails.

title: Process defects are countable, so a planner can ask how well the system is working

(1) Not countable by class: 'how many spec defects' means reading prose, and the precedent against exactly this is already in the repo - EVENT_OPS carries 'decision' as its own op with the stated rationale that a decision needs no text matching. (2) Bound to one spec: these are properties of the PLANNING SYSTEM, not of the run, so when that spec closes the only handle is --spec on a spec nobody will think to query. (3) No denominator, which is the one that decides the design: 'how well is the system working' is a RATE, not a count, and 5 defects means nothing without 5-across-how-many-dispatches. The denominator is already derivable from the log - specs written, clauses authored, work-prompts issued - so only the numerator is missing. Precedent for shape: spec-add/spec-remove/spec-defer/spec-done is already a family of four fine-grained ops rather than one op with a subtype field, so one op per class matches the house style. title: a closed record cannot be reopened, so a closure made against work that has not happened is unrecoverable
deliverable: Give a closed record a route back to open. c2 forbids refusing a write for a semantic reason and start's refusal is exactly that: the record's state disagrees with the caller, so the tool declines rather than recording what the caller asserted. Whether the verb is start accepting a closed record or a separate reopen is U3's to choose; what c2 requires is that one of them works.
evidence: Measured on a scratch copy of the store at f0936dc, so nothing was mutated: 'tasks start pass2-c-m3 --store <copy>' exits 1 with 'error: pass2-c-m3 is declined, not open' (scripts/tasks.ts:639), and 'tasks stop' exits 1 with 'error: pass2-c-m3 is declined, not in-progress' (:672). No other verb moves a record out of done or declined; the dispatch table has no reopen. This is not hypothetical on this branch. Twenty records were declined across 9637c24 and 44b9c1e, every one of them before a single deletion had landed, with reasons written as predictions. Thirteen were re-checked against the tree at f0936dc and eleven hold outright. Two do not: pass2-c-m3 and tasks-check-reports-freeze-warnings-for-specs-belonging-to-o each route a residual to doctor, and U3 has not run - pass2-c-m3 subject is live at scripts/tasks.ts:133 today. That ratio is the problem rather than the exception: closing ahead of the work is cheap and usually right, so it keeps happening, and the times it is wrong the store has no way to take it back. The decision pass2-c-m3 carried was re-homed into policy-seam-u3's evidence for exactly this reason - it was the only move available.

evidence: SETTLED 2026-07-29, promoted from .scratch.md. title: resolve() can stop checking that a boundary is not in the past and the whole suite stays green
deliverable:
A case in the "resolve: forward progress" block that drives that state through
  resolve() and asserts the RuntimeError names the resource and both instants. After it, removing
  or weakening the not-past call is a red test rather than a silent change, and c4's proof covers
  the loop and not only the pure rule.
evidence:
Mutation c4-loop-stops-calling-the-not-past-rule replaced the call at
  src/runtime/runtime.ts:365 with "void requireBoundaryNotPast;" and SURVIVED after escalating
  from src/runtime/resolve.test.ts to the whole suite — 1815 tests, the only failure the
  pre-existing audit.test.ts one. The two halves either side of the call are each observed: the
  rule dies to "< now - 1", and the call executes, since shifting its argument to "before + 1"
  is killed. It is the call's PRESENCE that nothing watches. And the state that would trip it is
  constructible end-to-end with the injection the spin test already uses: npm run inspect over a
  registry whose pool has rate: -0.001 per minute, an on empty handler and an injected level of
  0.5 milli-units, resolved to 5000, throws "resolve: resource pool put a boundary at -29999,
  before the current instant 0". c4 is the clause whose whole argument is that a claim is worth
  exactly what the assertion checking it is worth; a line that can be deleted with the suite
  green is that same claim one level up.

title: Three of the four names a stall report can carry are asserted nowhere, and each is built as a string on the path that never throws
deliverable:
Make Boundary carry a discriminated source — buff / action / resource / requested,
  each with its id — and format the message at the throw site through one pure function a test
  can call for all four shapes. That puts every name a report can print under an assertion, and
  as a side effect stops the never-read string from being built per candidate.
evidence:
Mutations c1-buff-boundary-is-misnamed, c1-action-boundary-is-misnamed and
  c1-requested-time-boundary-is-misnamed each replaced a Boundary source with the literal
  'something'; all three SURVIVED at whole-suite scope. Only "resource ${resource.id}" is
  asserted, by the spin test's /resource pool/. The action source is the one a real report is
  most likely to carry — the zero-length step the guard tolerates IS an action boundary, which
  STALL_BOUND 0 proves by killing that test — and it is unasserted, so the message c1 promises
  could name the wrong thing and no test would say so. Separately, and measured rather than
  assumed: the source is built at every candidate, including one template per nextBoundary call
  whenever an action is active, for a value read only when the guard throws, and the buff scan
  moved from Object.values to Object.entries. Over 2000 buffs at 2000 iterations that costs
  637ms against Object.values' 512ms, so at the buff counts a session actually reaches it is
  microseconds and is not a performance defect — it is an allocation on the hot path that buys
  nothing until something throws.

title: The boundary-source residual is assertable at the seam, so the argument for accepting it does not hold
deliverable:
Either export nextBoundary (or a thin named seam over it) from src/runtime and
 assert, for each of the four candidate kinds, that the winning Boundary carries the source that
 candidate is supposed to attach — four small pure-function cases, no guard needs to fire — or
 state in the spec's Decisions that the source label is diagnostic-only and deliberately untested
 for three of four kinds, so the next pass stops re-deriving it. This extends the already-filed
 which-candidate-a-boundary-s-source-names-is-unasserted-for- rather than duplicating it: that
 record's deliverable was "accept, unreachable"; this one says the assertion is cheap and reachable
 and should be written. Merge it as a note on that record if triage prefers.
evidence:
I mutated the wiring itself, at whole-suite scope. In src/runtime/runtime.ts,
 `source: { kind: 'buff', buffKey: key }` -> `source: { kind: 'requested' }` SURVIVED
 [src/runtime/resolve.test.ts -> whole suite], and `{ at: toTime, source: { kind: 'requested' } }`
 -> `{ kind: 'buff', buffKey: 'unwired' }` SURVIVED the same way; the action arm came back UNSTABLE
 at whole-suite scope (the spawn flake polluting that run), which is neither verdict. The control
 proves the measurement is sound: the resource arm's wiring ->  `{ kind: 'requested' }` is KILLED at
 file scope by two named tests. So the residual's SUBSTANCE is confirmed. What is wrong is its
 argument. The fixer wrote that buff, action and requested "provably never reach either guard from
 engine-produced state"; the action source demonstrably DOES reach requireForwardProgress — the
 mill fixture's zero-length segment passes an action-sourced boundary through it on every run, which
 is precisely what STALL_BOUND -> 0 kills. What is unreachable is the guards' THROWING path, and
 that is a different claim. It also does not support the conclusion drawn from it: nextBoundary is a
 pure function of (state, registry, toTime), so which source it attaches to which candidate can be
 asserted directly without any guard firing at all. The residual was accepted on the ground that no
 assertion could be built; one can, in about six lines.
reason: Merged as a note onto which-candidate-a-boundary-s-source-names-is-unasserted-for-, which is the same defect and already carried the reproduction; this pass's contribution was refuting that record's 'unreachable' argument, and it now lives there as a correction to its deliverable. title: printEvidence is a second spelling of wrapUnder, and EVIDENCE_WRAP_WIDTH is a hand-computed copy of the width wrapUnder derives
deliverable: printEvidence's body becomes evidence.split newline flatMap wrapUnder(line, EVIDENCE_INDENT), keeping its 12-line cap, and EVIDENCE_WRAP_WIDTH goes away. One wrap-and-indent in the file instead of two, and the width stops being a constant that must be edited whenever TERMINAL_WIDTH or EVIDENCE_INDENT moves.
evidence: EVIDENCE_INDENT is 10 spaces and EVIDENCE_WRAP_WIDTH is TERMINAL_WIDTH - 10 = 68. wrapUnder(line, EVIDENCE_INDENT) computes Math.max(TERMINAL_WIDTH - 10, 24) = 68 and, because hanging defaults to a run of spaces the length of first, applies the identical prefix to every line. The two produce the same output by construction. This branch introduced wrapUnder into the same file and converted spec show and handoff to it, leaving printEvidence as the one wrap-and-indent loop still written out by hand - so the duplication is the sweep stopping one caller short, not pre-existing drift.

title: summarize dropped its bound instead of replacing it with a wrap, so a brief record now prints a 2171-character line

evidence: Measured: 'tasks next --spec tool-friction-backlog' emits 11 lines, one of them 2171 characters. Before this branch summarize ended in truncateLine(text, 100). The comment now on summarize argues 'a prose line has no structure under it for that wrap to destroy', but in the brief rendering that prose is the value half of a labelled field printed among files:, writes: and produces: lines, so its soft-wrapped tail lands flush at column 0 against the next label - the exact shape wrapUnder was added to prevent. printEvidence, reached from triage, already wraps the same field to 68 columns, so the repo now answers 'how do I show a task's evidence' two different ways.

title: the record caps bound how many rows roadmap prints, but the id lists inside a row are uncapped, so one row's height is not
deliverable: The three id lists a roadmap row can carry - 'holds N: <ids>', 'waits on <ids>' and '(also waits on <ids>)' - take the treatment waiterNotes already gives unblocks: print the first few and say 'and N more'. The pattern and its constant (WAITER_CAP) already exist in the same file, so this is applying a decision the branch already made, not adding a concept. c10 promises the view states what it left out; today these three lists are the only display paths that leave nothing out and can still run to any length.
evidence: Measured on this branch. A synthetic 80-record store - one spec holding 40 members, each requiring the same 40 unspecced records - renders a 62-line DECIDED section for that single spec and a 402-line UNSPECCED section, 476 lines total, from a store one sixth the size of the real one. blockerText joins every blocker with no cap, the 'holds N:' list joins every member, and Waiter.alsoWaitsOn is built by waitersOf with no cap and printed in full by waiterText; only waiterNotes caps, at WAITER_CAP=3. Before this branch the same lists were held to one line each by fit()/truncateLine, so removing the character cut (c12) is what made their length visible as height. Not a regression - the pre-branch renderer printed all topics uncapped and was worse on the same store - but c10's bound is only over records, not over a record.

title: wrapUnder computes its wrap budget from the first-line prefix and ignores the hanging indent it applies to every other line
deliverable: wrapUnder budgets from Math.max(first.length, hanging.length), with a render.test.ts case wrapping under a hanging indent wider than its first prefix and asserting every line stays inside TERMINAL_WIDTH. Cheap now, and it converts a silent over-width into an invariant the type of the function already implies. This is also the signal that the wrapping helpers are worth revisiting: the first caller that wants a continuation indented deeper than its head is the moment, and until then the current shape is fine.
evidence: Measured: wrapUnder('word '.repeat(30).trim(), '  ', ' '.repeat(60)) returns lines of length [76, 134] - the second is 56 characters past TERMINAL_WIDTH=78. The budget is Math.max(TERMINAL_WIDTH - first.length, MIN_WRAP_WIDTH), so a hanging indent longer than first is added on top of a full-width line. No caller today trips it: tree, entryRow and clauseStandingLines all pass hanging.length === first.length, specLines passes hanging <= first because column() floors the state cell at STATE_COLUMN, and blockedLines errs the safe way (first longer than hanging, giving short lines). So the invariant holds by coincidence across five call sites and is neither documented nor tested.

title: Run an orchestrator over three parallel tasks
evidence: The controlled run the author asks for before an orchestrator prompt is written: you cannot brief a role whose failure modes you have not seen. Reframed 2026-08-06 - the point is ENDURANCE, not cost. Cost is settled by delegation-experiments.md. The constraint is that supervising a worker costs the author half a day, nearly all of it reading output and saying continue, while a planning session yields a dozen specs in the same day; with 17 specced tasks and ~30 findings waiting, the human is the bottleneck and every mid-branch design question is paid at the expensive rate. So the run measures how many times a human had to enter the loop and whether planning could have prevented each entry - not wall-clock, not audit counts, not cold-start versus reused context. Corpus is the three sibling prerequisites, whose grants are disjoint. The orchestrator is a buffer that batches everything non-decisional; the orchestrator brief itself is generated afterwards, the way plan-prompt, work-prompt and audit-prompt already are.

title: `checkSave` never looks inside the three fields that have an inside, and `loadSave` crashes on them with a `TypeError`
evidence:
**Verified, two reproductions.** `save.ts:38-52` gives every save field a `holds` predicate. For
the ten scalar- and number-shaped fields it is a real check. For the three object-shaped fields —
`activeAction`, `player`, `activeBuffs` — it is `isObject`, which is to say no check at all. Those
are exactly the three fields with internal structure to get wrong.

The rule the file states for itself (`save.ts:28-29`):

> "A `# save` body is hand-written JSON that nothing else checks, so this is where a
> `"time":"potato"` is caught."

It catches `"time":"potato"` and misses the class that actually crashes:

| `# save` body (version 5) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `{"time":"potato"}` | `RuntimeError: save field time holds "potato"…` ✅ |
| `{"activeAction":[]}` | `RuntimeError: …not what activeAction keeps` ✅ |
| `{"activeAction":{}}` | **`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'indexOf')`** |
| `{"activeAction":{"ownerRef":"entity.oven","actionLabel":"bake","repeating":false,"healthRemaining":1000}}` | **`TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`** |
| `{"player":{}}` | accepted; `state.player.name` is `undefined` thereafter |
| `{"activeBuffs":{"k":{}}}` | accepted, then silently pruned as "its stat undefined is not loaded" |

The first crash is `parseOwnerRef` (`save.ts:115`) on an absent `ownerRef`. The second is the
interesting one: **every id in that body is real.** The owner exists, the action label exists, so
`activeActionProblem` has nothing to prune and reaches `Object.keys(active.cadences)`
(`save.ts:127`) on an absent `cadences`. Nothing downstream can recover, because the crash is
inside the validator.

That the intent was the opposite is explicit two lines earlier: `activeActionProblem` wraps
`findActionOwner` in a `try/catch` that converts a `RuntimeError` into a warning and rethrows
anything else (`save.ts:119-122`). The author was thinking about precisely this conversion and it
is defeated by the next statement. A validator that throws a raw `TypeError` on the input class it
exists to validate has not validated it — and this is the only gate between hand-written JSON and
the resolver, since `06c2e47` routed `pruneStateForRegistry` through it for browser and disk saves
too (`scripts/play-cli.ts:320`).

**Fix**: `holds` for these three needs to be a real structural predicate, not `isObject` — for
`activeAction`, at minimum a string `ownerRef`, a string `actionLabel`, and a `cadences` object
carrying `PLAYER`. That is the same shape `activeActionProblem` already assumes; it just has to be
asserted before the assumptions are used rather than after.

title: `attemptDuration`'s floor gives one authored value three different fates
evidence:
`Math.floor(timeMs / speed)` (`stats.ts:53`) can now reach 0 for any positive `time:`, which the
pre-conversion float division could not. What happens next depends on which path reads it:

| Path | `duration === 0` |
| --- | --- |
| `armAction`, repeating | `RuntimeError` at arm time (`runtime.ts:404`) |
| `applyDueBoundaries`, deterministic non-repeating | treated as instant and completed (`runtime.ts:315`) |
| `resolveStochasticSegment` | **`RuntimeError` thrown mid-resolve** (`runtime.ts:215`) |

Reproduced for the third row with `time: 1, speed: 2000`: the action arms clean, `useAction`
resolves a zero-length first unit without complaint, and the next `resolve()` that crosses any
span throws `action entity.dummy.poke resolved a non-positive attempt duration (0)`. No load-time
check is possible because `speed` is state-dependent, so the three fates are the whole story.

Unreachable in shipped content — a 60 s action needs a speed stat above 60,000 — which is why this
is LOW rather than higher. It is listed because the divergence is not a decision anyone made; it
is what the floor did to three call sites that each already handled zero their own way.
reason: Self-described unreachable in shipped content, low severity.

title: `resourceRateRemainders` is never cleared when a resource stops having a rate
evidence:
`settlePools` writes the remainder only under `if (snapshot)` (`effects.ts:146`) and `continue`s
past a resource with neither snapshot nor delta (`effects.ts:140`). A remainder accrued while a
buff supplied a rate therefore survives the buff indefinitely and is re-applied if the rate ever
returns. Bounded at one minute's accrual — under one milli-unit — because the resolver forces a
boundary at every rate change, so this is cosmetic in the pool itself. It is visible, though:
`resourceRateRemainders` is a save field, so the stale value is serialised and compared by
`compareSave`, and a `# save` fixture recorded either side of a buff expiry will carry it.
reason: Self-described as cosmetic/bounded, low severity.

title: `PlaySession.logCursor` no longer carries information, and the one place it could is a nested session
evidence:
`9922073` made `view()` clear the log outright (`session.ts:192-194`), setting the cursor to 0 on
every read. Every other assignment — `startSession:169`, the `load` directive at `:345`, and
`runTest:369` — can now only produce 0 in a session that has ever called `view()`. The field
survives as a parameter that is always the same value.

The exception is the reason to mention it: `runTest` builds a *second* `PlaySession` over the
caller's state (`session.ts:369`). If that inner session reaches `view()` — a `begin:` directive
does, via `beginAction` — it clears a log the outer session is still holding a cursor into, and
the outer `state.log.slice(session.logCursor)` then silently returns nothing. Unreachable at
today's cursor values, which is exactly what makes it a trap rather than a bug: the invariant that
saves it is "the cursor is always 0", which no name or type records.
reason: Self-described as unreachable at today's values, low severity trap.

title: the `# test` regressions cannot see the largest change in the window
evidence:
**Verified by mutation.** I dropped `toMilliUnits` from `initResources` (`effects.ts:81`), so
every pool initialises at 1/1000 of its intended level, and ran the shipped content:

```
✓ test "tutorial-island.tutorial-quest-given" passes
✓ test "tutorial-island.miki-route-full" passes
✓ test "tutorial-island.save-restores-object-owned-flags" passes
× tutorial-island health resource (Pass 2 end-to-end) …
```

All three `# test` sections pass with every pool off by 1000×, including `miki-route-full`, whose
`expect: miki-route-end` compares the whole save diff. The only thing that fails is a hand-written
TypeScript assertion at `integration.test.ts:40`.

The cause is in the fixture `2c2ccee` migrated. `miki-route-end` carries
`"resources":{"tutorial-island.health":0}` — zero is the single value invariant under a scale
change, so rescaling it was a no-op and the fixture pins nothing about the new scale. `time` was
rescaled `107.2` → `107200` and *does* discriminate, which is why a seconds/milliseconds mixup
would be caught and a units/milli-units one would not.

CLAUDE.md designates `# test` sections as *the* regression format. For the largest change in this
window that format certified nothing, and the mechanism — a fixture whose only pool value is the
one value the transformation fixes — will recur on the next scale change unless a fixture pins a
pool mid-range.
reason: Symptom of already-deferred dsl-load-path-2026-07-30-pass2-h1; same root cause and fix.

title: `ability:` means two different numbers depending on which fight path reads it
evidence:
**Verified.** One module, one stat `blow` at `2.5`, two actions differing only in `health:` vs
`target: health`. Four attempts each, starting from 100:

```
healthless (deterministic) path:  100000 -> 90000   = 2.5 per attempt
target:    (stochastic)   path:  100000 -> 92000   = 2.0 per attempt
```

A 20% difference from the same authored number. The deterministic path takes
`toMilliUnits(statValue(action.ability))` (`runtime.ts:72`) and is exact; the stochastic path goes
through `hitDamage`, which is `Math.max(minDamage, Math.trunc(attack - dr))` (`stats.ts:47`) and
quantises to whole units before `damagePool` converts up.

The `Math.trunc` predates this window, so the asymmetry is not new — but the integer conversion
made the healthless path exact while leaving the target path quantised, which widens the gap
rather than closing it, and it is the sort of thing a conversion touching every damage site was
the natural moment to reconcile. This is a measurement for the `action.health`/`target:`
unification that pass-1 L4 and L6 are both blocked on: the two paths do not merely differ in
bookkeeping, they deal different damage.

title: `rng` is the one number in `GameState` the conversion left un-integered, and a fractional cursor collapses the stream
evidence:
**Verified.** `SAVE_FIELDS` validates `time` and both pool records with `isInteger` and `rng` with
`isNumber` (`save.ts:48-49`). Since the pass-2 H1 fix, `nextRandom` is
`(Math.imul(cursor.rng, MULTIPLIER) + INCREMENT) >>> 0` (`rng.ts:14`), and `Math.imul` applies
`ToInt32` to its arguments. So a save carrying `"rng":0.5` is accepted, and:

```
draws from rng=0.5    : 0.0000028742942959, 0.8275770242, 0.6524071617, 0.8374803169
draws from rng=12345  :                     0.8275770242, 0.6524071617, 0.8374803169
```

Every fractional cursor truncates to the same integer and lands on the same fixed stream one draw
later. Two saves that differ only in their `rng` fraction produce bit-identical futures. The
window's own work makes this worth fixing rather than tolerating: `5f3708d` built `SAVE_FIELDS` as
a `Record` over an exhaustive key type specifically so a field could not be forgotten, and the
table is exhaustive over *names* while remaining loose about *values* — which is the same root as
H1. `rng: isInteger` is a one-word change.

title: A pool saturated in its rate's direction loses its carried remainder, so where a span is split changes the level
deliverable: resolve() is associative for a pool sitting at its ceiling with a rate pushing into it, so a regenerating foe gives the same level and remainder however the span is cut, from the first instant rather than from the first hit.
evidence: Measured by audit pass 2 on combat-continuation-runtime, span 0-13s, foe stamina regenerating at 7/min: one shot gives level 36516 remainder 40000; split at [0.5,1.2,4,9,13] gives 36458 / 20000. settlePools zeroes the carried remainder whenever the write clamps (effects.ts, the 'clamped' branch), and enterEncounter stands every foe up AT its ceiling, so this is the opening condition of every fight against a regenerating enemy rather than an edge case. Pre-existing for the player — resolve.test.ts picks horizons that leave pools 'mid-range rather than saturated where any two answers agree' — but foes had no rate before this branch, so it became reachable here. enemy-pool.test.ts opens its span at OPENS=2 to step past it.

title: Migrate DSL-stored saves with one command per version bump
evidence: The half of save-migration-system that is useful to US rather than to users. loadSave refuses any version that is not exactly SAVE_VERSION and there is no migration, so every save-breaking branch forces each # save fixture in content to be regenerated by replaying its whole route live. Four such branches are queued — first-class-modals turns pendingModal into a stack, buffs-generalized may hold buffs per actor, items-mods-and-crafting adds instances, and unify-action-health-into-target drops healthRemaining. A one-shot command run at each bump rewrites the fixture's SHAPE; regeneration is still required when a branch changes BEHAVIOUR, and the two are not substitutes. This is a tool, not a maintained ladder: it does not have to keep old versions loadable, which is what makes it cheap before the core is settled.

title: A stale SHAPE_CHANGE from the previous bump is indistinguishable from this bump's declaration, and the one test that would notice turns itself off in exactly that state
deliverable: The declaration carries the SAVE_VERSION it was written for and migrate refuses one whose version is not the current one, with the same message shape it gives an unset transform. That makes c4's promise per-bump rather than per-file, and it keeps the refusal path reachable at every bump, so the subprocess seam test stops needing skipIf and the command's argv handling, exit code and disk behaviour are exercised at the only times the command is ever actually run.
evidence: Mutation `c4-the-shipped-shape-change-is-a-stale-declaration-rather-than-null` replaced `export const SHAPE_CHANGE: ShapeChange | null = null;` with a non-null transform that moves a field (`moved: (body) => ({ ...body, rng: 1 })`) and SURVIVED, measured at whole-suite scope: 1 failed of 1815, the same one already failing before it. Nothing in the suite notices that the shipped declaration is a stale field move rather than null. Two things make this more than a missing assertion. First, the workflow the spec's Decisions describe is "one exported value, overwritten by the next bump" and nothing enforces the overwrite or a reset to null; c2 does not help, because after a bump every fixture is behind and none is skipped, so the whole set takes the previous bump's transform. Second, the only end-to-end test of the refusal — scripts/migrate-saves.test.ts:238, the one subprocess test in the file, which is also the only check that main() writes nothing and exits 1 — is `it.skipIf(SHAPE_CHANGE !== null)`, so it is green-by-skip exactly when SHAPE_CHANGE is wrong. c4 exists to stop "I forgot to write one" reading as a declaration; a value the last bump left behind is that same failure with a declaration sitting in front of it, and the command cannot tell the two apart.

title: c3 validates the in-memory body rather than the bytes it is about to write, so a transform that drops a field the natural way is refused
deliverable: Validate `JSON.parse(rewrite.text)` — what the file will hold — instead of `rewrite.body`. One expression, and it makes c3's "each rewritten body is checked by loading it" true of the bytes rather than of the object they were serialized from, closing both directions at once: a transform whose output does not survive JSON round-tripping can no longer pass validation, and `{...body, field: undefined}` stops being refused for a value that would never reach the file.
evidence: Probed with `npm run inspect` against a one-module fixture. A transform returning `{...body, location: undefined}` — which is how a bump that drops a field reads most naturally, and the spec's own task evidence names `unify-action-health-into-target drops healthRemaining` as one of the four queued bumps — is refused with "alpha.here: save field location holds undefined, which is not what location keeps". The text that would have landed is `{"version":6}`, because JSON.stringify drops undefined keys, and a save is a sparse diff against initialState so an absent field is a valid default. The refusal names the fixture rather than the transform, so the author of a future bump is pointed at content that is fine. The workaround (destructuring the key out) exists but is not discoverable from the message. NaN and Infinity are caught today, so this is over-strictness rather than a bypass, which is why it is low; the same one-line change is what makes both directions follow from the bytes.

title: Nothing exercises the precedence rule that makes a recording beat an input, which is the only thing standing between c5 and a rewritten recording that is never named for regeneration
deliverable: A fixture in migrate-saves.test.ts that a `# test` both `load:`s and `expect:`s, asserted to classify as a recording and to appear in the /create-valid-test line whichever order the two directives are written in. That pins the rule the `&&` guard implements instead of leaving it as an unexplained condition a later simplification will remove.
evidence: Mutation `c5-a-fixture-that-is-both-loaded-and-expected-is-downgraded-to-input` dropped the `&& found.get(directive.save) === 'unreferenced'` guard from the `load:` branch of classify() and SURVIVED at whole-suite scope: 1 failed of 1815, the same one already failing before it. The guard is what makes 'recording' final once set, so without it a fixture a test both loads and expects is classified by whichever directive is read last. Every fixture in the test module is named by exactly one directive, so nothing reaches the case. The behaviour is correct as written; what is missing is the test that says so, and c5 is the clause that pays if it is ever simplified away — a recording silently reclassified as an input is a recording that gets rewritten in shape and never named for /create-valid-test, which is the one confusion c5 exists to prevent.

Re-run against the post-deletion tree at f0936dc on clause-1, verbatim, store confirmed unchanged after each: 'tasks decline <id> --reason ...' exits 1 with 'error: <id> is undelivered and cannot be declined' (scripts/tasks.ts:769); 'tasks spec remove task-system-real-world-friction-spec <id>' exits 1 with 'error: undelivered task(s) cannot be removed from a spec: <id>' (:989); 'tasks done <id> --commit HEAD' exits 1 with 'error: <id> is undelivered and proof clause 1 is not met in the latest audit pass (pass 1)' (:696); 'tasks drop <id> --because ...' exits 1 with 'unknown command: drop' (:1843). spec done --defer-open was not re-run: it writes across every member of the superseded spec and its refusal is already recorded, so re-measuring it risks a partial write for no new information. title: The store is rewritten whole with no lock, so a concurrent write loses records and a concurrent read answers short
evidence:
`saveStore` (`scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:481`) is `writeFileSync` over the entire 1.4 MB file. Every
write verb is `loadStore` → mutate → `saveStore`: no lock, no compare-and-swap, no staging file, no
re-read.

**Lost writes.** Eight concurrent `tasks add` against a copy of the live store: eight `added …`
lines, zero errors, eight `add` events in `docs/events.jsonl`, **three records on disk**, and
`doctor` reports 0 errors. Independently reproduced at three writers: three successes, one record.
Staggering shows the window — 0 s offset loses records, 0.2 s offset does not — so the hazard is
precisely "writers dispatched together", which is what an orchestrator does.

**Torn reads — and this is the mechanism behind the reported symptom.** `writeFileSync` truncates
and then streams; a reader inside that window sees a *prefix*. When the prefix ends on a newline
every line in it is valid, so `parseStoreTolerantly` — which `readStore` uses for every read
command — has nothing to report. Measured with two writers and one reader loop:
`reads 1826, reads answering short 1825, short reads with no skip message at all 803,
fewest records seen 0`. Write window p50 2.89 ms / max 9.95 ms against a 3.40 ms read.

That is a store that is short, self-consistent, silent, and exit-0 — which is exactly
*"agents are constantly reading the store and discovering stale or incomplete information."*
The symptom is not stale records. It is a truncated file.

`docs/workflow.md:135-140` states the write hazard in prose and tells humans to serialise filing by
hand. It understates it in two ways: it does not mention reads at all, and **nothing detects the
loss afterwards** — `doctor` never opens the event log, so the one witness that kept all eight
records is never asked. Reconciling the two live files directly finds 4 ids the log knows and the
store does not.

**Fix, in order of cost.** Ten lines in one function: write to `.tmp` and `rename` (atomic, ends the
torn read), and re-read-and-compare before writing (ends the lost write). No caller changes. This
retires H8's persistence, M6, the manual serialisation rule, and the reason §6.1 exists.

title: The git seam destroys the reason for every failure, and four call sites turn "git could not answer" into a positive claim
evidence:
`scripts/lib/git.ts` is a disciplined seam: fifteen facts, every one nullable, twenty-five tests
pinning what "git said no" looks like — unborn HEAD, no merge base, unreachable rev, buffer
overflow. The layer above spends that discipline. `raw()` (`scripts/lib/git.ts:38-42`) sets
`stdio[2] = 'ignore'` and discards the exit code, so **fifteen distinguishable failures arrive as
one indistinguishable `null`**, and four of the twenty-two call sites coalesce that `null` into a
benign default (`?? []`, `|| '(none)'`).

Consequence: `merge-ready` can print `tree ok — pass, nothing uncommitted` and "the base has not
moved" in a directory where git cannot answer at all.

The same shape repeats as bare `catch { return null }` — **15 swallowed catches across 9 files** in
the non-test region. In every one the reason exists for exactly one stack frame and is then
destroyed. **No subprocess in the region sets a timeout, anywhere.**

This is the direct answer to *"the system fails to reliably log its own errors."* It does not fail
to log them. It destroys them at the seam, one frame after they are known, and then answers
confidently from the default.

title: Flag arity is parsed out of documentation prose, so two commands accept a flag they do not have
evidence:
`flagArities` (`scripts/tasks/cli.ts:27`) is a regexp over the usage *string*, and this repository's
usage strings carry rich explanatory parentheticals. The guard against prose applies only to the
token *after* a flag, never to the flag token itself — so any `--word` named inside a parenthetical
enters the accepted vocabulary with an arity read off the next English word.

Reproduced:

```
$ npm run tasks -- list --trigger "some condition"
… entire unfiltered list …                                              exit 0
$ npm run tasks -- list --nonsense foo
error: unknown flag: --nonsense
  `list` takes: --state, --severity, --system, --spec, --kind, --deferred, --unspecced, --triggered, --trigger
```

`--trigger` belongs to `decline`, not `list`. The value is silently discarded **and the refusal path
advertises the flag by name.** Same for `tasks decision "…" --op note`. A sweep over all 41
registered verbs finds exactly `list: [trigger]` and `decision: [op]`.

`scripts/tasks/context.ts:9-11` and `scripts/tasks/commands.ts:203` both promise *"a flag not named
there is an error, never a silent no-op."* A declared arity table beside each usage string — one
line per command — makes both promises true and makes `reportUnknownFlags` exact rather than
prose-derived.

title: A repeated flag silently keeps the last value
evidence:
`scripts/tasks/cli.ts:90` — `flags[key] = value` into a `Record<string, string>`. There is nowhere
for a second value to go and nothing notices one arriving.

```
$ npm run tasks -- list --state open --state declined
222 task(s) — … declined: 222
$ npm run tasks -- list --state declined
222 task(s) — … declined: 222
```

Identical, exit 0, no message on either stream. An agent writing `--state open --state in-progress`
to mean a union gets a plausible, complete-looking, wrong list. Same class as H12: one rule — *every
argument the parser accepts must reach the command body, or be an error* — closes both.

title: `doctor` classifies nine conditions as `error` and exits 0 on every one of them
evidence:
`scripts/tasks/doctor.ts:97-101` is the only non-zero path and it fires on unparseable lines alone.
But `checkStore` (`scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:785-819`) does not classify along malformed-versus-
semantic; it classifies `error` versus `warning`, and its `error` set is dominated by **broken
references**: a system name not in `systems.json`, a spec with no file, a `requires` naming nothing,
a duplicate id, a dependency cycle.

Those are not disagreements about the work. They are the store having drifted out of sync with the
tree — precisely the staleness class this audit exists over. Every one is reported and none fails
anything. The behaviour is pinned by its own test (`scripts/tasks/doctor.test.ts:10-23`), which
asserts `status === 0` alongside `[error] a has a system not in systems.json: Nonexistent`.

A record filed under a system name that does not exist is invisible to every `--system` query —
which is the reported visibility failure with the field left blank instead of wrong. Making the
*reference* errors fail (and leaving the semantic warnings reporting) would make the CI leg the
first automated check in the repository that a record still points at something real.

title: `tasks log` reports "no events recorded yet" over a log whose every line failed to parse
evidence:
`scripts/tasks/handoff.ts:85` branches on `events.length` alone. Its own comment two lines above
argues that an empty log and a filter matching nothing are different answers — and then collapses a
third case, *the log exists and none of it parsed*, into the second.

```
$ printf 'not json\n' > <scratch>/events.jsonl
$ npm run tasks -- log --store <scratch>/tasks.jsonl
no events recorded yet in …\events.jsonl
skipped 1 unreadable event line(s) — everything above is the rest of the log: …
exit=0
```

The store draws this three-way distinction correctly at `scripts/tasks/context.ts:161-173`. One call
site catching up with a pattern the region already has.

title: `merge-ready`'s `tree` leg is red at exactly the moment the gate is meant to run
evidence:
`scripts/tasks/mergeReady.ts:155-160` fails on any dirty path — which is the state the documented
merge procedure guarantees, since the gate is run before committing. The comment three lines above
(`:149-151`) denies that the leg fails at all. Its own test asserts that it does.

A leg that is red by construction trains every reader to discount the gate's output, which is the
one output that is supposed to be read literally.

title: A write grant is a promise with no observation point, and it is graded at the one moment nobody could have kept it
evidence:
Three separate defects, one mechanism. See §4.1 for the full reproduction.

1. `resolveGrant` (`scripts/tasks/records.ts:78`) honours `--grant commitment` unconditionally and
   cannot tell `add` from `edit`, so a planner can record a commitment on a region nobody has read.
   All three Phase 3 records were born `commitment` at planning commit `8c12842`.
2. `checkPlan` runs once, before dispatch, when the grant's measured accuracy is 10–50%. The
   corrected grant arrives during the run and nothing re-grades it. `tasks edit --writes` already
   calls `reportPriorArtOnWrites`, which *did* name the collider — as line 59 of 233 lines of
   untagged prior art.
3. `task.grant` is read at five non-test sites and `writes` is compared to a real diff at none.
   Neither `tasks start`, nor `tasks done --commit`, nor `merge-ready` ever asks whether the branch
   wrote what it promised.

**Fix.** Refuse `--grant commitment` on a record that has never been started. Call `checkPlan` from
inside `reportPriorArtOnWrites` and print defects *above* the prior-art wall, so the check fires at
the moment the record becomes true. And have `tasks done --commit <rev>` report grant-versus-diff:
it has both in hand, the workflow already asks a human to do it by eye, and recording the delta is
also the only cheap answer to §6.8.

title: `tasks where` discards same-system callers, so the one query that could show a sibling caller is blind exactly where siblings live
evidence:
`regionView.importedBy` (`scripts/lib/architecture.ts:244`) filters callers down to cross-system
ones. Fifteen files in the tree import `scripts/tasks/context.ts`; `tasks where
scripts/tasks/context.ts` prints none of them — including `scripts/tasks/auditPrompt.ts:568`, the
exact call site left behind when `a8fd3e6` narrowed `resolveActiveSpec`'s body, which produced the
`merge-ready` / `audit-prompt` deadlock.

`tsc` cannot catch this class and neither could a deleted-export detector: the signature at
`scripts/tasks/context.ts:219` is unchanged. Only the body narrowed. The break is behavioural with
no type surface, which is why the branch's own by-hand survey of all seven callers enumerated
`auditPrompt.ts` and classified it "informational WARNING/no-op, never a write, never a pass
filer" — a classification that was wrong, in the direction of harmless, and that nothing checks.

**Fix.** Delete the `byPath.get(to)?.system !== candidate.system` clause and label cross-boundary
callers instead of filtering to them. One clause.

title: A record's `system` is never checked against the system that owns its own paths
evidence:
`--system` is validated only against the list of names in `docs/audits/systems.json`
(`scripts/tasks/context.ts:339-347`). `ownerOf` (`scripts/lib/systems.ts:172-181`) is a pure
function over the already-loaded manifest that resolves a path to its owning system, and is already
used for the reverse direction by `tasks where` — and never for this.

Reproduced: `tasks add … --system "Testing procedure" --writes scripts/lib/taskStore.ts` succeeds
with **zero warning**, while printing 33 lines of prior art on that file, nearly all of it filed
under "Task system".

Surveyed over the live store: of 146 open records carrying both a system and at least one path,
**8 are clean, unambiguous mis-filings** — every path resolving to one system, and not the declared
one. Four of the eight are task-system tooling records filed as "Testing procedure", which is the
same failure as the flagship case:

`every-system-owns-its-files-by-name` — the record whose deliverable is *"stamp the freeze SHA onto
the Task system entry"* — is filed `Testing procedure` / `medium`, and is confirmed absent from
`tasks list --system "Task system" --severity high`. It is also `kind: task`, so `roadmap`'s
"FINDINGS — could redden an audit" section would never show it either.

The previous orchestrator diagnosed this exactly, in a `note` event attached to that very record,
and the record's fields were never corrected. **A correct diagnosis recorded next to the defect it
describes is not a fix.** That is the clearest single argument in this audit for enforcing rather
than narrating.

**Fix.** One warning-level comparison — `task.system` against
`ownerOf` over `writes ∪ files` — added either to `reportPriorArtOnWrites` (stops new ones at
authorship) or to `checkStore` (catches the eight already filed). Both is better. A warning, never
a refusal: some records legitimately span systems.

title: `clauseStandings` is reconciled against the store at two of nine call sites
evidence:
`clauseStandings` (`scripts/lib/specDoc.ts:286`) takes the *document's current* clause list and
returns verdicts only for ids still in it. Two callers — `scripts/tasks/mergeReady.ts:337-342` and
`scripts/tasks/records.ts:794` — separately rebuild the clause-id set from the store's own
`discharges`/`clause` fields and fall back to `unknown`. The other seven, including the
human-facing `tasks spec show`, do not.

Reproduced twice in a scratch fixture:

- **Deletion.** Removing a graded clause's bullet from the markdown makes `tasks spec show` print
  `clause standing (composed over 1 pass(es)): no clause outstanding` two lines above a member list
  still showing that clause's task as `[undelivered/open/high]`. `doctor` reports 0 errors.
- **Rewording.** Rewriting a clause's text while keeping its `[c1]` tag silently reattaches the old
  verdict to the new text, while the undelivered record keeps the original snapshot. Two live,
  disagreeing statements of what clause 1 is.

**Fix.** Make `clauseStandings` take the store's clause ids as a required input, the way
`mergeReady.specStanding` already had to invent for itself. Closes all seven sites in one change.

title: `--args-from` classifies a line by its prefix rather than by parser position, so an audit files silently corrupted evidence
evidence:
`parseAuditFile` (`scripts/tasks/audit.ts:240-259`) drops every blank and `#`-prefixed line
unconditionally (`:245`) and treats every `--`-prefixed line as a new flag unconditionally (`:246`),
whether or not a value is currently open. `AUDIT_USAGE` documents the rule as "any unprefixed line
continuing the value above it" and mentions neither carve-out.

Reproduced twice, both exiting 0 with a success message:

- A `#4521 for background…` line mid-evidence is **silently deleted** from the filed record.
- A `--file 3=src/example.ts:10 and confirm the crash` line mid-evidence truncates the evidence and
  lands its tail in `files[]` as a bogus reference with an embedded newline.

This is the silent sibling of the already-open `task-system-refactor-pass2-b-l1` (an `--evidence`
beginning `<digits>=` is captured as clause evidence). That one refuses loudly; these two file
successfully with corrupted data. `--args-from` is the **one filing route for a branch audit**, so
this is the mechanism by which an audit's findings get quietly lost.

**Fix.** Track parser position: only classify a line as a flag-opener at top level. One change
retires all three manifestations.

title: 104 of 792 records share a `seq`, and `seq` is the sole tie-break in every queue
evidence:
Measured on the shipped store: 792 records, 727 distinct `seq`, **39 colliding values across 104
records**. `nextSeq` (`scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:491`) is max+1 over what one branch can see, so two
branches produce the same number.

`seqRank` is the only tie-break in all four queues. Reversing the input array diverges `listQueue`
at index 17 of 171 and `unreviewedQueue` — the queue `tasks triage` walks — at index 9 of 27.

`scripts/lib/orderIndependence.test.ts` exists to forbid exactly this and passes, because its
fixture gives every record a distinct `seq` — a precondition its own header states at line 9 and
the live data violates 104 times. The comment at `scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:493` calling collisions
"harmless, because `seq` orders a queue and does not identify a record" is false: ordering a queue
is the entire job it has, and `:519`'s "oldest first" is actually id-alphabetical for those 104.

**Fix.** Either make the tie-break total (`seq`, then id) — two lines, and it makes the existing
test's property true of the live data — or take `seq`'s job back to the event log's own append
order under §6.1.

title: A duplicate id answers two different ways inside one command
evidence:
`resolveIds.ts:21` uses `Array.find` (first match); `scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:572` builds
`new Map(pairs)` (last match). Reproduced with one id present twice: `tasks show zz-dup-dep` prints
`[task/done]` while `tasks show zz-waiter` prints `requires: zz-dup-dep (waiting)` — two answers,
one store read. `tasks edit` reaches only the first copy and `saveStore` writes both back forever.
`doctor` reports `[error] duplicate id` and **exits 0**.

`.gitattributes:14-16` justifies excluding the store from `merge=union` on the stated grounds that
"every read answers from the first copy forever". Every `byId` read answers from the last. The
reasoning that shaped a merge strategy is wrong about the behaviour it was reasoning about.

There are zero duplicate ids in the store today; this is a latent hazard, not a live one.

title: `CLAUDE.md`'s own wisdom line has drifted from the tested source it was copied from
evidence:
`CLAUDE.md:26` — *"Enforce where a value is assembled, not where it is **written**"*.
`scripts/tasks/briefLessons.ts:85`, printed into every planner brief and pinned verbatim by
`scripts/tasks/planPrompt.test.ts:106` — *"Enforce where a value is assembled, not where it is
**read**."*

"Assembled" and "written" are the same moment, so the governing document's copy states nothing. The
tested copy states the lesson. See §4.3 for the nine other relations of this shape and §4.4 for why
this one is the exhibit.

title: `work-prompt` re-asserts the grant kind as unconditional prose after printing it correctly
evidence:
`printGrant` (`scripts/tasks/workPrompt.ts:54`) renders the actual grant; `printObligations`
(`:112`) then tells every worker its grant is a forecast, thirty lines later, regardless.

title: The concept-overlap report prints case-folded keys as if they were paths
evidence:
`scripts/lib/systems.ts:255-260` — `audit-status` reports `scripts/lib/specdoc.ts` and
`scripts/tasks/auditprompt.ts`, which name nothing on a case-sensitive filesystem.

title: A never-swept system has no change volume to report
evidence:
`scripts/audit-status.ts:65` derives "commits changed since last sweep" from `lastAudit`, so the one
system with `lastAudit: null` — the Task system, until this document — is the one the report says
nothing about.

title: Nine verbs and the interactive triage walk each hand-roll the same wrapper
evidence:
Nine of `records.ts`'s sixteen `cmdX` functions (`scripts/tasks/records.ts:712-1123`) repeat
resolve-ids → precheck → mutate → save → record-events → print, and `scripts/tasks/triage.ts:36-96`
carries a second independent copy of five of them. The domain logic underneath is genuinely shared
(`transition`, `writeAskedQuestion`, `pass2Promotion`); only the plumbing is duplicated. One
`applyRecordChange` parameterised by precheck/mutate closures would collapse ~280 lines to ~90 plus
a ~40-line helper, and would let the interactive forms call the same path as the batch verbs.

title: No command answers "what is open about this file"
evidence:
`tasks where <path>` prints prior art across every state with no `--state` filter; `tasks list`
filters by state/severity/system/spec/kind with no path filter. Nothing joins them — which
compounds H4, since `list --system <owner>` is unreliable when the `system` field itself may be
wrong.

title: `check-commit-msg` is absent from the CLI's own root usage line
evidence:
`scripts/tasks/commands.ts:20`'s hand-maintained `USAGE` constant omits a real, working verb. Every
other summary in that file is derived from the `COMMANDS` table; this one is not.

### 5.9 Confirmed, already filed — not re-filed

| existing record | what this sweep adds |

| `the-generated-mutation-manifest-expands-one-file-only-target` (unreviewed/high) | Quantified: `a-branch-is-told-which-spec-it-owes.md` generates **684** entries, `a-move-never-strands-a-question.md` 507, against 28 for a spec using quoted per-test targets. **0% usable** — every entry ships an unaimed sentinel. Hand-built replacements in 5+ consecutive passes at 10–30 min each. |

| `triage-writes-state-directly-in-three-places-bypassing-trans` (open/low) | **Already fixed** by `2ed2f96`; the record is stale and should be closed. Its `files` field still names `scripts/tasks.ts`, now a 12-line shim. |
| `max-lesson-count-is-a-quota-of-the-shape-claude-md-retired-o` (unreviewed/medium) | **Refuted.** It is enforced (`auditPrompt.test.ts:1017-1021`) and it measures a flat count, not the gameable ratio the comment budget measured. Recommend declining. |
