title: one bad SHA silences the whole ledger, and the hook reads the crash as "nothing to report"
evidence:
`touchesSince` (`scripts/audit-status.ts:83`) runs `git log <lastAudit>..HEAD` through
`execFileSync` with no guard. Setting Testing procedure's `lastAudit` to `deadbeef`:

```
Error: Command failed: git log --format=%h %s deadbeef..HEAD -- scripts/play-cli.ts …
fatal: bad revision 'deadbeef..HEAD'
    at touchesSince (scripts/audit-status.ts:83:15)
```

The 2026-07-28 pass logged this as **L1**, "crashes with a Node stack trace" — cosmetic, because
the crash still exits non-zero. It was never fixed and never lifted into `backlog.md`. `7676c09`
then changed what non-zero *means*:

```bash
case "$ledger" in
  *"audit due:"*|*"no audit doc:"*) ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac
```

A stack trace carries neither verdict line, so the hook classifies it as "the ledger could not
run" and exits 0 **without writing the state file**, so it re-reaches the same conclusion on every
subsequent commit. Measured, with the ledger reachable (the worktree's `audit-status` script
repointed at the parent's `tsx`):

| Ledger state | Hook exit | State file written | Reported |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OK | 0 | `<head> ok` | — |
| genuinely DUE | 2 | `<head> due` | yes |
| `lastAudit: deadbeef` | **0** | **none** | **no** |
| `deadbeef` **and** threshold 1, so another system is genuinely due | **0** | **none** | **no** |

The last row is the one that matters. The crash happens inside the per-system loop, so no verdict
line for any system is ever printed, the `audit due:` summary never runs, and **`orphanedFiles`
never runs either** — it sits after the loop at line 131. One unresolvable SHA disables commit
counting, the doc gate and the partition check together, and the only thing that still notices is
CI at push time.

This is not hypothetical: `lastAudit` records a branch SHA, and this repo rebases and squashes
feature branches. Once the original is gc'd the reference is unresolvable.

Same class, same consequence: a malformed `systems.json` throws out of `JSON.parse` at line 106,
before the loop.

Fix is two small ones. In `audit-status`, resolve `lastAudit` with a `try` and turn a failure into
a named verdict line (it already has `undocumented` as the template for "a system is
mis-recorded"), so the ledger reports rather than aborts. In the hook, treat an unrecognised
non-zero exit as worth one line on stderr rather than silence — fail-open is defensible for a
missing `node_modules`, but not for a ledger that ran and blew up.
reason: Fixed: confirmed in pass3's "What this window got right" (closed alongside pass-2 H1).

title: `/create-test` is the one authoring command that ignores the authoring machinery
evidence:
`11d9335` gave the REPL a real local-DSL path: `/dsl <kind> <id> <body>` stages a section through
`upsertLocalSection`, reloads the universe to prove it valid, and persists via
`writeLocalChanges`. `play-cli.test.ts:508` demonstrates it authoring all sixteen section kinds
local-changes may own — **including `# test` and `# save`**.

`buildCreateTest` (`play-cli.ts:241`) predates that and was not revisited. It hand-assembles the
block, `console.log`s it, and mutates `session.registry` in place
(`registry.tests.set`, `registry.saves.set`) without ever touching `authoring`. The recorded
regression exists only in the terminal scrollback until a human copies three blocks into a content
file by hand — which is the exact step CLAUDE.md's "record a regression as a `# test` section via
`/create-test`" is supposed to make cheap, and the exact step `/dsl` already automates.

It is also the only writer that bypasses the load-time validation gate: `/dsl` refuses a section
that does not load, `/create-test` cannot refuse anything because it never re-loads.

Routing `buildCreateTest`'s three blocks through `commitLocalChanges` deletes the duplicated
registry mutation, gives `/create-test` the same validation and persistence every other authoring
verb has, and makes the emitted test survive the session. It also removes the mechanism behind
**H1**'s worst outcome, since a corrupt emission would then have to survive a reload.
reason: Real gap but lower priority than the already-deferred H1 in the same area.

| `deadbeef` | `     Testing procedure  0 of 0 commit(s) …; 0/2 completed task chunk(s)` | **0** | **accepted** |

The same fixture against `4631baa`'s `audit-status.ts` exits **1** with a Node stack trace. So the
change converted a loud failure into a green one.

Three consequences, not one:

- **CI passes.** `test.yml` runs `npm run audit-status`; exit 0 is a passing step.
- **The chunk budget reads 0 forever.** It is now the *verdict* — `audit-status.ts:186` is
  `owed || budget.state === 'block'` — so the system can never become due again.
- **`tasks done` stops refusing.** `doneTask` (`tasks.ts:757-762`) calls the same
  `auditBudgetForSystem`. The block that the design calls "the forcing function" is off, silently,
  for that system only.

Git's own `fatal: bad revision` reaches stderr, but it carries no verdict line, so `audit-due.sh`
classifies the run as successful (`if ledger=$(npm run --silent audit-status 2>&1)` succeeds),
writes `<head> ok`, and never speaks — the same fail-open the previous pass logged as **M1**.

This is not hypothetical, and pass 1 said why: `lastAudit` records a branch SHA and this repo
rebases and squashes feature branches. Once the original is gc'd the reference is unresolvable.
**M1's task is still open and its prescribed fix is the right one** — resolve `lastAudit` in a
`try` and turn a failure into a named verdict line alongside `undocumented`, so the ledger reports
rather than either aborting or lying. The window applied the `try` and skipped the verdict line,
which is the half that carried the signal.
reason: Fixed: confirmed in pass3's "What this window got right" (closed alongside pass-1 M1).

title: the chunk budget counts trailer lines, not chunks, so the number in `systems.json` is neither of the two things it could mean
evidence:
`auditBudgetForSystem` (`tasks.ts:483`) is
`commits.reduce((sum, commit) => sum + commit.trailers.length, 0)`.

For `task-system` in this window the six trailers are:

```
task-system#1  task-system#1  task-system#6  task-system#6  task-system#6  task-system#7
```

- declared chunks in the task (`git show 92adffe:docs/tasks/task-system.md`): **8**, all checked
- distinct `(task, chunk)` pairs closed by a trailer: **3**
- reported by `audit-status` and `--brief`: **6**

Three numbers, none equal. Chunk 6 was committed three times and counted three times; chunks 2–5
and 8 were closed without a trailer and counted zero. The design's stated unit is
"a chunk of a completed task, not a commit" (`task-system.md:323`), rejecting commits precisely
because "a commit is an arbitrary slice". Counting trailer occurrences restores the arbitrary
slice — a session that splits one chunk across three commits spends three times the budget of one
that does not. `parseTaskTrailers` also accepts a bare `Task: <id>` with no `#n` (`tasks.ts:452`),
and that counts 1, which is a commit counted as a chunk by construction.

The same mechanism blinds `--brief`. Its "Completed tasks in range" is derived from trailers
(`audit-status.ts:143`), so **31 of the 32 `done` tasks naming Testing procedure have zero trailers
anywhere in history** and are invisible to it. The brief for this audit listed one completed task;
two were confirmed at `9adc928`. `go-full-integer-milli-units-and-integer-milliseconds` charges
this system per the design's multi-system rule (`task-system.md:127-130`) and contributes nothing
to either the count or the auditor's working set.

Both halves are one fix: derive the count from the tasks (`status: done`, naming the system,
whose completion falls in the range) and their own checked chunks, using trailers to locate the
task rather than to be the unit. `tasks confirm` strips `## Chunks`, so the compacted archive
cannot supply the boxes — which is the constraint that pushed the implementation to trailers, and
the reason the fix has to decide deliberately rather than by default.
reason: Superseded by pass3-h1/h2, the current more-precise measurement of the same undercounting.

after:  file contains "LOAD-BEARING PROVENANCE LINE"  -> false

reason: Confirmed still open (pass3 scorecard) but latent — no task file currently carries pre-title content.

title: `npm run tasks` takes 19.5 seconds to compute a tiebreak that cannot discriminate
evidence:
`firstCommitTimestamp` (`tasks.ts:342`) spawns `git log --follow --format=%ct -- <file>` and is
called from inside `rankedQueue`'s sort comparator (`tasks.ts:371`) with no memoisation.

```
tasks list   real  0m19.484s
tasks check  real  0m0.240s
```

`rankedQueue` alone accounts for 19.6s of that. One `git log --follow` over this repo costs 0.142s,
which puts the comparator at roughly 138 spawns for a 48-item queue — the same file re-queried on
every comparison it participates in.

The value being computed is degenerate. Across all 94 tasks there are **8 distinct first-commit
timestamps, and 87 tasks share one of them** — the migration commit `ec4bc17`. So tiebreak 3
("oldest first") can order 7 tasks out of 94, and costs 80× the runtime of the CI gate to do it.

`tasks next` runs the same function, so `/task-next` — the command the slash-command prose makes an
agent's first action of every session — pays the full 19.5s. The function is pure per file; a
`Map<string, number>` in `rankedQueue`'s scope makes it 94 spawns worst case, and hoisting it out
of the comparator into a precomputed table makes it 94 exactly.
reason: Confirmed still open/worse but already tracked as its own item per pass3.

title: `systems.json` has two readers, two type declarations and two default-budget expressions in one process
evidence:
`audit-status.ts:116-117`:

```ts
const manifest = JSON.parse(readFileSync(MANIFEST, 'utf8')) as Manifest;
const taskStore = readTaskStore();
```

`readTaskStore` reads and parses the same file into `taskStore.manifest` (`tasks.ts:241,251`). Two
parses of one file on consecutive lines, producing two object graphs that are then used
interchangeably — `printBrief` takes its `system` from the first and passes it to
`auditBudgetForSystem`, which is typed against the second.

The declarations have already drifted. `audit-status.ts:8-14`'s `System` has five fields;
`tasks.ts:44-51`'s `SystemEntry` has six — `noFindings`, which gate 8 depends on and which
`audit-status` therefore cannot see. `git`/`safeGit` are duplicated verbatim
(`audit-status.ts:35-45` against `tasks.ts:108-118`). And the budget default is written twice:

```ts
// audit-status.ts:205 — what is printed
const budget = manifest.chunkBudget ?? { warn: manifest.threshold ?? 20, block: manifest.threshold ?? 20 };
// tasks.ts:474 — what is enforced
const budget = store.manifest.chunkBudget ?? { warn: store.manifest.threshold ?? 20, block: ... };
```

A manifest without `chunkBudget` gets its printed budget from one copy and its verdict from the
other. They agree today by having been typed twice.

CLAUDE.md's rule is *"do not create systems that are required to be manually kept in sync"*, and
this window is the one that wrote it into the file. `audit-status` already imports two symbols from
`tasks.ts`; importing `readManifest` — which is exported and has zero callers — and deleting the
local `System`/`Manifest`/`git`/`safeGit` makes the manifest have one reader.

title: the handoff hook fires on process commits, and blocked the first command of this audit
evidence:
`.claude/hooks/task-handoff.sh:46-54` reports any moved HEAD whose commit has no `Task:` trailer
while some task is `active`. Reproduced without trying: the first `npm run audit-status` of this
pass returned

```
HEAD moved to 9adc928… while a task is active, but the commit has no Task: trailer.
active task: combat
```

`9adc928` is *"confirmed two tasks"* — a `tasks confirm` bookkeeping commit that touches two task
files and no code. `combat` has been `active` since `ec4bc17` and no commit in this window is
combat work.

The rule is as specified (`task-system.md:192`), and the specification is what is wrong. `tasks
check` permits **at most one** `active` task, so any commit that is not that task's work — a
confirmation, an audit record, a `systems.json` edit, a merge, a revert, the commit that lands
*this* document — is structurally unable to carry a satisfying trailer and will trip the hook. The
first rule (trailer present, task file missing) is precise and worth keeping; the second is a
category claim derived from a field that means "a task is open somewhere", not "this commit should
have been task work".

It exits 2 on `PostToolUse`, so it interrupts rather than blocks, and its state file makes it
fire once per HEAD. The cost is not the interruption, it is that the design's own thesis —
"a warning is knowledge, and this project has demonstrated it already has the knowledge and loses
it" (`task-system.md:562-569`) — applies to a forcing function that cries wolf on routine commits.
The narrow version is to fire only when the commit touches a path the active task's system owns,
which `systems.json` already answers.

title: the chunk-budget fix under-counts the exact case it was written to fix: `task-system` weighs 1, not 8
evidence:
`the-chunk-budget-counts-trailer-lines-not-task-chunks` states its acceptance criterion as
"Proof is task-system reading 8 rather than 6" (`docs/tasks/the-chunk-budget-counts-trailer-lines-not-task-chunks.md:13`).
Measured with the store's own parser:

| revision | `task-system` chunks the parser sees | budget weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `92adffe` (pre-compaction) | **8**, all checked | — |
| `52013f2` (HEAD) | **0** | **1** |

`task-system.md` was compacted by `tasks confirm` *before* this window removed the stripping, so
its `## Chunks` section is gone from the file. `auditBudgetForSystem` (`scripts/tasks.ts:498`)
weighs it `task.chunks.length || 1` — the fallback, not the chunk list. Reconstructing the window
the finding cites:

```
lastAudit=4631baa → count 9: chunk-budget 3, unresolvable-lastAudit 2, one-bad-sha 1,
                             status-vocabulary 2, task-system 1
```

Three numbers were wrong before (8 declared, 3 distinct pairs, 6 reported). There are still three,
and the reported one moved further from the true one.

The load-bearing error is in the recorded decision
(`the-chunk-budget-counts-trailer-lines-not-task-chunks.md:57`):

> The 36 already-compacted tasks keep working: Chunks stays optional for a confirmed task rather
> than becoming required, so nothing needs migrating.

They keep *parsing*. They do not keep *counting*. `serializeTask`'s new
required-or-present filter (`scripts/tasks.ts:283-284`) is what makes them keep parsing, and it
works; but a task whose boxes were already deleted has nothing for the new counting rule to read,
and no migration chunk was written. The decision names this exact failure mode two sentences
earlier and calls it "a worse defect than the one being fixed":

> If its chunk boxes are gone the count for that task collapses to zero or to a fallback of one,
> which means the user's confirmation would silently lower its own system's audit debt

That is the shipped state for every task confirmed before `52013f2`. The population is frozen at
36 and will not grow, which bounds the damage — but `task-system`, this system's largest completed
deliverable and the finding's own worked example, is inside it.

Blast radius is small and precisely known. Of the 36 compacted tasks, 34 were migrated from

Exactly one is materially mis-weighted: `task-system`, 8 → 1. The fix is a one-time backfill, and
the data is recoverable — `git show 92adffe:docs/tasks/task-system.md` still has all eight boxes.

**Recommended fix, and it is not "restore the boxes":** see the note under M1. Freezing the count
into frontmatter at `tasks done` closes H1, H2 and M1 together and lets compaction go back to

reason: This task is no longer relevant after the audit budget system was retired.

reason: No longer relevant after the audit budget system was retired.

title: `task-system.md` still documents the contract this window replaced

title: a stray trailer now recharges an already-audited task's full chunk count; this is a regression against trailer counting
evidence:
Consequence of the same missing completion date, and it runs the other way. A task that completed
and was audited in a previous window stays `status: done` forever. Any later commit whose message
names it — a follow-up fix, a doc correction, a `tasks chunk` tidy-up — pulls it back into
`completedTasks` and charges its **entire** chunk count against the new window.

| | old behaviour | new behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| one stray `Task: old-task #3` in a fresh window | charges 1 | charges `old-task.chunks.length` |

For a task the size of `task-system` that is 8 of an 8-block budget from a single trailer line on
an unrelated commit. Trailer counting bounded this at 1 per line; chunk counting removed the bound
without adding the range filter that was supposed to replace it. Not observed firing in this
window — every in-range trailer belongs to a task genuinely completed in it — but it is one
follow-up commit away, and the failure is silent and blocks `tasks done`.

**The fix that closes H1, H2 and M1 at once.** Stamp the size and the date at completion:

```
status: done
completed: 2026-07-30
chunks-at-done: 8
```

`doneTask` already validates that every box is checked at exactly this moment, so it is the one
point where the count is known to be final and correct. Then the budget is "tasks whose
`completed:` falls in the range, summed over `chunks-at-done`" — no trailer involved. This
- makes compaction orthogonal again, so the pass-2 design change becomes optional rather than forced;
- freezes the count against later edits to the checklist, which the current rule does not;
- makes the 36 legacy tasks a one-pass backfill instead of a permanent blind spot;
- reuses the `confirmed:` frontmatter-stamp pattern already in the model rather than adding a mechanism.

It is strictly more of a change than what shipped. It is also the shape the design was reaching
for, and it retires three findings.
reason: No longer relevant after the audit budget system was retired.

| population | count | correct weight | weighed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| migrated-already-compacted (never had chunks) | 34 | 1 is defensible | 1 |
| compacted-after-having-chunks | 1 (`task-system`) | 8 | 1 |
| declared zero-weight by design | 1 (the container) | **0** | 1 |

The third is an explicit contract, not an inference. `testing-system-usable-and-reliable.md:37`:

> This task is a container, not work. It carries no chunks of its own and **spends no audit
> budget**; its `blocked-by` is the membership list.

It is `open` today, so nothing is wrong yet. When its 16 members close and it goes `done`, any
commit naming it charges 1 against a block budget of 8 — 12.5% of a window spent by a task whose
own spec says it spends nothing. The user flagged this; it is real, it is small, and it is a
contract violation rather than a judgement call, which is why it is M and not L.

Under the M1 frontmatter fix the fallback mostly disappears: `chunks-at-done: 0` is a real
recorded zero and needs no `|| 1` guess. If the current scheme is kept instead, the three
populations need three answers, and the container needs an explicit one.
reason: Self-described as latent ("nothing is wrong yet"); resolves once M1's fix lands.

title: `--round-trip` blames the wrong module when the universe contains a `# remove`
evidence:
`scripts/probe.ts:150-157`. The reload is `[...others, printed]`, where `others` are the *original*
sources. The printed module is serialized from the merged registry, so every other module's edits are
already baked in — and then those modules load again and replay their edits on top. Idempotent edits
survive that; `# remove` does not, because `registry.ts:594` throws when a removal names nothing
loaded.

Demonstrated. `base.dsl` declares `item rope` and `item bread`; `cut.dsl` is `# remove item.base.rope`:

```
base: its serialization does not load
  cut [cut] resolve: # remove item.base.rope names an unknown item: base.rope
cut: its serialization loads to a different registry
  items: added base.rope
```

`base`'s serialization is fine. The tool reports it as broken, in the exact words c4 reserves for a
serializer defect, on the branch's headline use case. Not a regression — `squash-local-changes.ts`
had the same reload-with-replay shape before this branch — but the new tool's claim is what fails.

title: `parseVitestTally` reads stdout+stderr and takes the last match, so a stderr line can invert the verdict
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:86-92` and `:255-259`. `runTests` builds `raw = stdout + stderr`, which destroys
ordering, and `parseVitestTally` takes the last `Tests` line. In vitest 4.1.9 the summary is on
stdout while the Failed Tests block and test-emitted output go to stderr, so any stderr line of that
shape wins.

Demonstrated on real captured bytes from a test that `console.error`s a tally-shaped line and fails:

```
stdout+stderr (what runTests builds): {"failed":0,"total":999}
stdout alone (the truth)            : {"failed":1,"total":2}
```

`0 failed of 999` reads SURVIVED where the truth is KILLED; a `Tests 3 failed` decoy inverts it the
other way. Latent — nothing in the current suite prints such a line — but it is a silent inversion of
the tool's only output, and it compounds with M3, which discards the evidence that would contradict
it. The fix is to parse stdout only.

title: `declaredVariableIds` gained an unmeasured `.sort()`
evidence:
Not present in any of the three `variableIds` copies it replaced. Removing it SURVIVED against
`roundTrip.test.ts` and `serialize.test.ts`. Redundant at `squash-local-changes.ts:106`, which sorts

evidence:
`mutate.ts:98-100`. The sole justification for `split`/`join` over `String.replace`. Swapping it for
`text.replaceAll(...)`, which still replaces every occurrence but does reinterpret `$&`, SURVIVED the

title: the `no tests` branch is an equivalent mutant

`mutate.ts:90`. Deleting it SURVIVED, because the fallthrough already yields 0/0 on that input. The
test at `mutate.test.ts:213` cannot distinguish the branch from its absence. The format is real —

`mutate.ts:231,236`. `path.resolve(repoRoot, file)` lets an absolute path or `../..` mutate anything

unbounded as written.

evidence:
`probe.ts:187`. A mistyped filename prints a raw Node ENOENT stack trace where every other error path

evidence:
Captured bytes live only in process memory, which is the design's selling point and its single point
of failure: a SIGKILL or a closed terminal during the window leaves the tree mutated with no recovery
path, and by construction git cannot help, because the premise is uncommitted work. The usage text
documents the window but not that outcome.

evidence:
A compile-breaking run went 1074 to 1027; 47 cases silently stopped running and the report said only
`3 failed of 1027`. Capturing an unmutated tally once and flagging a drop would make that visible.

evidence:
`probe.ts:125,130`. `loadUniverseWithDiagnostics` then `parseUniverse`. Harmless, and `parseUniverse`'s
throw is unreachable after a clean load, but redundant work on shipped content.

title: a throwing restore-write escapes `runMutations`, and the `unrestored` proof never runs
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:149-151` versus `:157-166`. The restore is `files.write(...)` inside `finally`. If
that write throws, the exception replaces the flow, the loop aborts, remaining mutations never run,

whose write fails only on restore: no report produced, file still mutated, second mutation never ran.

CLI's exit handler is a backstop but retries the same failing write and swallows the error, so the

title: `--show` cannot name `variable`, `flag` or `save`, and the comment justifying that is wrong
evidence:

title: the two fixes pass 1 rated HIGH are both unfalsifiable by the suite
evidence:
Measured with `npm run mutate`, whole-suite scope, baseline 1113, and independently reproduced:

```
h1-reload-originals        SURVIVED  0 failed of 1113  [whole suite]
h2-tally-reads-stderr      SURVIVED  0 failed of 1113  [whole suite]
probe-parsed-truncated     SURVIVED  0 failed of 1113  [whole suite]
registry-parsed-unordered  SURVIVED  0 failed of 1113  [whole suite]
```

`scripts/mutate.ts:353` is the H2 fix, `parseVitestTally(stdout)`. Reverting it to
`parseVitestTally(\`${stdout}${stderr}\`)` — the pass-1 defect verbatim — kills nothing, because
`runTests` is a `const` inside `main()` and only the `RunTests` *type* is exported. No test can reach
it. The fix is guarded by a three-line comment and nothing else.

`src/content/roundTrip.ts:42` is the H1 fix, `reload(sources)` where `sources` are the
serializations. Changing the argument to `reload(modules.map((each) => each.source))` kills nothing,
and that mutant makes `--round-trip` **always report clean** — the tool's entire purpose becomes
inert, invisibly. All five `roundTripUniverse` tests supply their own `reload` closure and assert on
what the closure does to the text it receives; not one asserts anything about the argument it was
handed. Commit `a7462c0` also deleted the only probe test that asserted `--round-trip` can report a
failure and replaced it with one asserting the opposite, so every remaining probe round-trip test
asserts `ok: true`.

This is the failure `docs/workflow.md` §6 exists to prevent, occurring in the branch that ships the
tool for preventing it. The branch author's report that "all ten fixes died" does not reproduce for
these two: the mutations run were of the adjacent pure functions — `parseVitestTally` itself, and a
reload argument that added a duplicate `# info` and so failed the load for an incidental reason —
rather than of the decision each finding was about.

Both are about five lines to pin. H2 wants `runTests` split so the stream choice is data:
`export function tallyOf(streams: { stdout: string; stderr: string }): TestRun`, which is the
"pass effects in as data" rule `runMutations` already follows and `runTests` does not. H1 wants the
test's reload closure to capture the sources it receives and assert they equal `result.sources`, plus
one probe-level test that `--round-trip` still exits non-zero on something.

title: a truncated journal permanently wedges `mutate`
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:309-310`. `JSON.parse(readFileSync(JOURNAL, 'utf8'))` is unguarded, and the
journal is written by one non-atomic `writeFileSync` carrying the full pre-mutation bytes of every
target — a wide window. A run killed during that write leaves a half-written journal, and every
subsequent run then dies before reading the manifest, before recovering anything, before restoring
anything:

```
SyntaxError: Unterminated string in JSON at position 69
    at main (scripts/mutate.ts:310:26)
journal still there? YES
```

The stack trace names `mutate.ts`, not the journal path, so the only escape — deleting an
undocumented file in `os.tmpdir()` — is not discoverable from the error. The recovery mechanism
becomes an unconditional crash in exactly the scenario it was added for.

title: journal recovery writes one checkout's bytes into another, bypassing the containment fix
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:236, 252-263, 315`. `JOURNAL` is one fixed path per machine carrying no record of
which repository root it was captured from. `recoverFrom` resolves every key against *this* process's
`repoRoot` and writes with no `escapesRoot` check — that fix is applied to `mutations` and not to
journal keys. Demonstrated with a dead-pid journal naming one relative and one absolute path:

```
recovered 2 file(s): zz-journal-victim.txt, C:/…/scratchpad/outside-victim.txt
--- zz-journal-victim.txt ---   BYTES FROM ANOTHER CHECKOUT
--- outside-victim.txt ---      WRITTEN OUTSIDE THE REPO ROOT
```

Two worktrees of this repo on one machine: a run in A is killed, and the next run in B silently
overwrites B's files with A's bytes and calls it recovery. Not hypothetical — `.claude/worktrees/` is
in vitest's exclude list because worktree-isolated agents are how this repo parallelises. Key the
journal filename by a hash of `repoRoot`, store the root inside it and refuse a mismatch, and run
`escapesRoot` over journal keys before writing.

title: `restoreFailures` is unproven
evidence:
Deleting `|| restoreFailures.has(file)` (`mutate.ts:179`) SURVIVED at whole-suite scope, because the
M2 test's throwing write also leaves the bytes wrong and the byte-compare catches it alone. Pinning
it needs a store whose write throws *after* landing the bytes; otherwise the condition is either dead
or a guard against a case nobody has named.

title: pid reuse wedges the busy check
evidence:
`journalVerdict` (`:247-250`) compares only `pid`, while `startedAt` is recorded and never used. A
recycled pid reads as permanently busy. The message tells the user to delete the journal, so it
degrades to a documented manual step, but comparing `startedAt` would close it for free.

title: `UniverseRoundTrip.printed` carries a second meaning on an inherited field
evidence:
`roundTrip.ts:41`. It is a `// --- name ---`-labelled concatenation of every module, and is not
loadable — multiple `# info` gives "declares # info more than once" — yet it inherits the field name
and type from `RoundTrip.printed`, where `printed` is the reloadable text. Computed on every call;
probe never reads it; one test asserts on it.

title: `alive()` treats EPERM as dead
evidence:
`:300-307`. A `process.kill(pid, 0)` EPERM is treated the same as ESRCH, so a journal held by a live
process owned by another user reads as dead and gets recovered.

title: the journal is plaintext source in a world-known path
evidence:
`:372`. Full source bytes in `os.tmpdir()`, left there whenever `unrestored` is non-empty. Per-user
tmp on Windows makes this minor, but it is uncommitted work at a predictable location.

title: the corpus-count test forces a hand-edit per archived audit
evidence:
`scripts/lib/auditImport.test.ts:100,110` pins exact finding counts across `docs/audits/`.
Pre-existing, not this branch's doing, but this branch is the first to pay it twice, and CLAUDE.md
names manual-sync systems specifically.

title: `--round-trip` can silently cover only some of the universe
evidence:
`scripts/probe.ts:140`. `loaded.parsed` to `loaded.parsed.slice(0, 1)` SURVIVED at whole-suite scope.
c4 promises "serializes every loaded module"; nothing tests that the set is complete, so that half of
the mechanism is as unpinned as the other. A patch module dropped from the reload is invisible
precisely because patch modules serialize to nothing.

title: the ordering contract on the new public `UniverseLoadResult.parsed` is prose only
evidence:
`src/content/registry.ts:89-91, 725`. `parsed: [...ordered].reverse()` SURVIVED at whole-suite scope.
The comment claims "in the order they were applied" and nothing checks it. This is a cross-system
change — a new non-optional field on the load path's most widely consumed result type — with no test
of `parsed` anywhere under `src/content/`. `roundTrip.test.ts` calls `parseUniverse` separately rather
than using it, so the handoff the field exists for is exercised only through `probe.ts`.

title: the baseline pass runs before the manifest is validated
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:358-368` against `:370`. `refuse()` is pure and needs only `files.read`, but runs
inside `runMutations` after N full test runs. A one-character indentation error in a `find` cost four
baseline runs, about 90 seconds, and then `applied nothing — the manifest was refused`. c7's
guarantee still holds; the ordering is backwards for cost.

title: the report cannot say a verdict had no baseline
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:194, 365-367`. If a baseline run throws, `shortfall` is `undefined` and
`formatReport` renders nothing — byte-identical to a verdict that had a baseline and no shortfall.
The only notice is one stderr line during the preamble, and the report is on stdout, which is what
gets pasted into an audit. This is c8's own argument: a `SURVIVED` measured without a baseline is a
weaker claim, and the report does not distinguish them.

title: the journal is not a lock; two runs can both start
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:309` to `:330`. Between the `existsSync` check and the write sit the recovery
branch and the pre-read of every target. Two runs launched together both see no journal, both
proceed, the second clobbers the first's journal — destroying its only recoverable copy — and both
mutate one tree. `writeFileSync(JOURNAL, …, { flag: 'wx' })` with `EEXIST` as the busy path makes it a
real lock. Reasoned from the code, not raced.

title: `--show`'s vocabulary is split between DSL kinds and registry map names
evidence:
`scripts/probe.ts:25, 94`. `--show variable.travel-seconds-per-unit` is refused;
`--show variables.travel-seconds-per-unit` works. The accepted list is nine singular authoring kinds
and three plural internal map names in one undifferentiated row. `# variable` is what the DSL says,
so the natural guess is the wrong one. Pass 1's M5 is half-closed: the records are reachable, under a
name the author never types.

title: the lazy baseline is measured on the mutated tree
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:167-172, 185-187, 461-477`. `measure` calls `baselineFor`, and `measure` is called
from `runMutations` *after* `files.write(mutation.file, applyTo(...))`. Both the narrow and the wide
baseline are therefore taken with the mutant on disk. Instrumented:

```
narrow saw MUTANT
  baselineFor(narrow) ->
narrow saw MUTANT
whole  saw MUTANT
  baselineFor(whole) ->
whole  saw MUTANT

verdict: SURVIVED | total: 25 | shortfall: undefined
Truth: 40 tests run unmutated, 25 mutated. The shortfall is 15.
```

End to end, breaking `roundTrip.ts` so one file cannot collect:
`breaks-collection-of-one-file KILLED 3 failed of 1086` against a suite of 1153 — 67 tests silently
stopped running and the row says nothing, because the whole-suite baseline was itself measured at
1086. The poisoned value is memoised and reused by every later mutation in that scope. The usage text
still claims "Each distinct test scope is run once unmutated first", which is no longer true.

This is the class of bug the shortfall exists to catch, and it is reachable: a mutation that does not
compile produces `Tests 0 failed` at narrow scope, because vitest 4 counts a collection failure on
the `Test Files` line only, which `parseVitestTally` never reads. `total === 0` does not fire, so the
verdict is SURVIVED, and the one remaining guard — the test-count drop — is exactly what the poisoned
baseline suppresses. The tool then asserts a coverage gap that does not exist. Two fixes are needed:
take the baseline before the write, and read `Test Files ... failed` so an uncollectable file is an
ERROR rather than a verdict.

title: `--round-trip=module` reintroduces the defect commit 7b16910 fixed
evidence:
`scripts/probe.ts:123-140`. `canSerialize` has exactly one call site, in the universe path, and the
guard was not carried into the module path.

```
$ npm run probe -- snippet.dsl --round-trip=module
snippet: publishing this module alone would not preserve the universe
  items: missing rock                                            <- exit 1

$ npm run probe -- snippet.dsl --round-trip
not round-tripped: snippet declare no # info ...                 <- exit 0
```

`7b16910`'s commit body, verbatim: "`--round-trip` on a source with no `# info` reported
`items: missing rock`, which reads as a serializer defect. It is not." The new mode reports exactly
that for the same input. The principle that commit named — a check that could not run is not a check
that failed — is violated in the new path, and no module-mode test covers a source without `# info`.

title: one pre-existing red test turns every escalated verdict into a false KILLED
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:156, 470`. The verdict compares `run.failed > 0` against zero rather than against
the baseline's failure count, and `baselineFor` records `.total` only. This existed before c14 but was
rare, because the whole suite had to be chosen deliberately. Now narrow scopes are the recommended
default and every survivor is pushed into the full suite, where any unrelated red test lives. A false
SURVIVED gets investigated; a false KILLED closes the question and records coverage that is not there.
The whole-suite baseline already runs unmutated — recording its `failed` and refusing to escalate on a
red tree costs one field.

title: `readJournal` accepts `root: ""`
evidence:
`path.resolve('') === repoRoot` whenever mutate runs from the repository root, which is the normal
invocation, so the root-mismatch check passes for a journal with an empty root. Defence-in-depth only,
since the path is hash-keyed.
reason: speculative edge: nothing constructs an empty journal root, and the journal is per-checkout so a wrong path cannot cross checkouts

title: `STALE_AFTER_MS` treats a long-running run as a reused pid

Six hours. Run B recovers A's files out from under A mid-run, deletes A's journal and takes the lock.
A 30-mutation whole-suite battery is not far off that. Comparing `startedAt` against the holding

title: `journalPathFor` hashes the root string without case normalisation
evidence:
On Windows, the same checkout reached by two differently-cased paths yields two journals and no mutual
exclusion. Hard to trigger given `import.meta.dirname`, but this is a Windows-primary repo.

title: `refusalsFor` runs twice per invocation
evidence:
Once in `main` and again inside `runMutations`. Harmless, but the ordering guarantee the pass-2 fix
bought lives only in `main`, where no test reaches it — the same structural shape as pass 2's H2.
reason: refusalsFor is pure and measured in milliseconds; caching it trades a correctness risk for no observable win

title: `main()` is untested as a composition
evidence:
Every extracted decision is now pinned; their composition is not. H1 lives at the `main` call site,
although `measure` and `runMutations` are exported and could have caught it.

title: `escalatedFrom` is lost when the escalated run throws
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:188-189`. `runMutations`'s catch rebuilds the result from `scopeOf(mutation)` with
no knowledge of what `measure` had established, so the reader sees an ERROR against the narrow scope
and cannot tell the mutation survived that scope and then the whole-suite run blew up.

title: a refused manifest leaks the journal lock
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:456-459` exits without `rmSync(JOURNAL)`. Demonstrated: after a refusal the journal
survives, and the next run reports "a journal from an interrupted run was found". Three consequences —

your tree" fires routinely after every typo'd manifest, which is how a real warning becomes invisible;
and a second run started while the first is alive refuses with "another mutate run is holding this

title: the narrow verdict's shortfall is discarded by escalation
evidence:
`scripts/mutate.ts:170-171` returns `{...wide, escalatedFrom}`, replacing everything measured narrowly.
The disagreement between narrow and wide is the most informative thing an escalation produces — it
names the file missing a test — and the row keeps only the wide half.

title: module mode's diagnostic relocates the pass-1 blame rather than resolving it
evidence:
`scripts/probe.ts:130`. `base: its serialization does not load beside the others` names the artifact
and its failure and invites the pass-1 misreading, while its own sibling line
`cut: publishing this module alone would not preserve the universe` names the action and its

deliverable: A dev-only window.__test exposes named actions registered by the components that own them plus a structured state read, and takes a batch of commands in one round trip returning one result per step. A production build contains no trace of it.

Second, c11's scoping is correct but unproven: a hand-built mutation on ownClauseIds -- scoping changed records to ownMembers before computing owed clauses -- SURVIVED at whole-suite scope, because no test declares two specs in one branch diff with overlapping clause ids. evidence: Both from pass 1 of a-branch-is-told-which-spec-it-owes. The deadlock was reproduced independently by the orchestrator on claude/spec-declared at b8f96d3 and is filed as audit-prompt-still-asks-resolveactivespec-whether-the-branch. The surviving mutation is the auditor's own, run at whole-suite scope, and is the reason c11 is graded met on its literal text but proven by nothing -- mergeReady.test.ts:607 covers one spec with several members, never two specs at once.

title: The browser save store adapter
deliverable: The named-slot store's browser implementation, over localStorage: the same interface the file-backed one satisfies, so autosave, export, import and the dev slot behave identically in the GUI and the REPL. A quota failure, a disabled-storage browser and a slot written by an older build are each a message rather than a lost session.

There is one slot-store interface, owned by a-named-slot-store-with-a-written-at-stamp, and this is an implementation of it -- the new capability is that the game persists in a browser at all, which is the question a later survey will actually ask.

title: The CLI fixture answers git from data, and a call site that wants the real repository says so
The command set lives below the UI layer
deliverable: One table below the ui layer names every command, its argument shape and its handler; dispatch is a lookup in it and no driver holds or filters a command of its own. /help is computed from that table and HELP_LINES is gone. A command result carries the resulting view and the messages the command produced, with no terminal vocabulary below the driver. The live clock tick moves down with it. play-cli keeps the readline loop, the bars, the glyphs and the numbered list, and its observable behaviour is unchanged apart from /help.

title: The five remaining repository-per-case test files reach their assertions without one

deliverable: A file-only proof target should produce ONE manifest entry whose kill scope is the file, not one entry per test declared in it. c1 of brief-builds-the-manifest says a file-naming target 'resolves to the tests declared in those files', and the worker met that literally: audit-prompt on this five-clause spec now writes 354 entries -- 72 each for c1/c2/c3 (every test in auditPrompt.test.ts) and 69 each for c4/c5 (all of audit.test.ts). A file-only target does not know WHICH test in the file a clause is about, so expanding it 72-fold multiplies that judgement rather than supplying it. The clause's own property sentence -- 'a target resolves to whatever the auditor would run for it' -- is better served by one entry per file, since running a file-only target runs the whole file. Deciding between those two readings changes what c1 promises and is a planning decision, not an orchestrator's or a worker's.
evidence: Raised from medium to high 2026-08-08 by the author, after it recurred. Measured three times independently. (1) The orchestrator before the pass-1 audit: 354 entries, 72 each for c1/c2/c3 and 69 each for c4/c5, across two test files. (2) The pass-1 auditor, unprompted and in use: found them impractical to hand-aim, built a six-entry manifest at a scratch path instead, and logged about 10 minutes lost -- against a deliverable that reads 'No auditor hand-builds a mutation manifest again'. So the friction the branch existed to remove is now paid by every auditor of a spec whose clauses name files, which is nearly every clause in this repository. Neither remedy the friction log proposes exists: npm run mutate takes exactly one argument, a manifest path, so there is no way to run a subset of a generated manifest by name; and audit-prompt applies no cap on how far a whole-file target expands. c1 is met in text and its deliverable is not met in practice, which is why the disposition is a clause decision rather than a defect fix.

title: The suite is deterministic with no worker cap, measured

title: The task store survives parallel branches
evidence: Measured 2026-08-06 against the real store, and the original narrative below it was wrong. Two branches editing different records merge CLEAN -- saveStore writes one record per line in canonical key order and never moves a line, so git's three-way merge already resolves edits per record. The only conflict is the tail hunk every branch appends to, and re-run id-sorted the same scenario merged with zero conflicts. The three candidate shapes the record originally named are all closed in the spec's Decisions: no merge driver (git config merge.<name>.driver is per-clone, so every worktree spawn needs a setup line), no .gitattributes entry (union is right for the append region and wrong for the edit region; sorting deletes the append region), and no event-log projection (events record which field changed, never the value). What is left is a sort, plus the thing the sort destroys: four queues tie-break on array index, so file position IS creation order, and 456 of 590 records predate the event log -- the reorder commit is the last moment that information exists.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 5: The residual is named where a reader will hit it. Two branches inserting adjacent ids conflict on one hunk with a new record on each side, and the resolution is to keep both; a test pins that this is the *only* remaining conflict shape, so a future one cannot be mistaken for it.
deliverable: The residual is named where a reader will hit it. Two branches inserting adjacent ids conflict on one hunk with a new record on each side, and the resolution is to keep both; a test pins that this is the *only* remaining conflict shape, so a future one cannot be mistaken for it.
evidence:
The named test (taskStore.test.ts:404) is real and passes: two branches each inserting a
new record between the same two existing ids conflict once, in the shape described. But the clause's
stronger claim — "a test pins that this is the *only* remaining conflict shape" — is false. I built an
adversarial real-git-merge scenario (spawnSync git, same pattern as the shipped tests, not mocked):
branch A edits an existing record (title change only, no id/position change); branch B inserts a new
record whose id sorts immediately adjacent to the edited one (zero untouched lines between them once
saveStore sorts by id) — merge exits 1, a real conflict, shaped as an edit on one side and an insert on
the other, not two inserts. I then swept the gap between the edited line and the inserted line from 0
to 6 untouched lines: gap=0 conflicts, gap>=1 merges clean (confirmed with the array's actual id used
for `saveStore`'s sort, not the array-splice position, which is irrelevant since saveStore always
re-sorts). I also confirmed a second new shape: one branch deletes a record while the other inserts a
record adjacent to the deleted one — also conflicts. So the true residual is "any two changes whose
lines land adjacent in the id-sorted file," which subsumes insert+insert but is not the same claim as
"two branches inserting adjacent ids" and is not limited to a shape resolved by "keep both" — an
edit+insert conflict must be resolved by reconciling the edit, which "keep both" does not describe.
This is realistic, not contrived: ids in this store are hyphenated slugs that commonly share a prefix
for related work (an audit's own finding ids are typically `<subject>-passN-...`), so a record being
edited and a new record about the same subject are likely to sort next to each other. Filed as finding
H1.

title: c4 and c5's dedicated "real merge" tests do not independently prove the property they claim under mutation testing: removing saveStore's id-sort survives at each test's own scope and is only caught by escalating to the whole test file, where an unrelated test (c1's) happens to catch it.

evidence: Ran `npm run mutate` against a manifest that disables saveStore's sort (scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:329, replacing the sort with a no-op `[...tasks]`), scoped first to each test's own name via `-t`. Both "two branches...merge with zero conflicts" and "the one residual...conflict once" report KILLED only after escalating from their own named-test scope to the whole-file scope (reported by mutate.ts itself as `"<test>" -> scripts/lib/taskStore.test.ts`), which mutate's own usage text documents as "not that clause proving itself." Root cause: both tests build the inserted/edited records by array-splicing at what is already the alphabetically-sorted position (e.g. inserting "r-04-mid" via `.splice(5, 0, ...)` into an already-ascending array), so saveStore writing them in whatever order the array already has produces the same bytes as writing them id-sorted — the mutation changes nothing observable to these two tests.

title: roadmap.ts's seq tie-break (added past c2's four named sites, for the roadmapView `topics` ordering) is unreachable: mutation-verified dead code under the whole 1667-test suite, not just its own test
deliverable:
Either demonstrate a real scenario where roadmap.ts:250's `|| seqRank(a.task.seq) -
seqRank(b.task.seq)` term changes topics' output and add a test that forces it (one where `unblocks.length`
reordering actually disturbs the seq-adjacency `listQueue` already established for same-severity entries),
or remove the term as dead and correct 137245b's writes-grant rationale ("closing a real tie-break") and
the-task-store-survives-parallel-branches's own claim that this generalization closes a position-dependence
gap in this file — it does not, currently, change any observable output.
evidence:
topics' input (`backlog`) is `listQueue(tasks, {...}).map(...)`, and listQueue already sorts by
(severityRank, seqRank) as its own final tie-break before topics ever runs. topics adds a new primary key
(`unblocks.length`) ahead of severityRank, but for any two entries where unblocks.length AND severityRank
both tie, JS's Array.prototype.sort is stable, so their relative order is preserved from `backlog` — which,
because they share a severity tier, is already seq order. The explicit seqRank term at roadmap.ts:250 can
therefore never change the result. Verified with `npm run mutate`: deleting
" || seqRank(a.task.seq) - seqRank(b.task.seq)" from roadmap.ts, scoped first to
orderIndependence.test.ts's own "roadmapView topics" test (which reverses its input array and expects the
same topics order) — SURVIVED, then escalated automatically to the whole file, then to the whole suite
(1667 tests) — SURVIVED there too, 0 failed. roadmap.test.ts's own dedicated tie-break test
("breaks a fan-out tie by severity, then by seq, oldest first, regardless of array order", added this same
branch to replace an array-order-coincidence test) also does not catch it, for the same reason: whatever
order it hands roadmapView, listQueue re-sorts by seq before topics' own comparator runs. producers.ts's
analogous priorArt fix does not have this problem — its comparator runs directly over the raw `tasks` array
with no upstream seq-sort, and the equivalent mutation there (removing its seqRank term) is KILLED, 1 of 6,
at "priorArt claims"'s own scope. This is not a live behavioural bug (roadmapView's actual output is
correct today, since listQueue already provides seq order); it is unverified, currently-inert production
code shipped under an explicit, coordinator-reviewed writes-grant widening (137245b) that names this file
as closing a real gap, which it does not appear to do.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 11: **Filing a record shows what already claims the path it names, and never refuses.** The prompt is by path and never by title, because a path is the same string for everyone while a title is authored prose two agents will not choose alike — `priorArt` already reads every record's `writes` and `files` in every state, so this is wiring, not a new query. Attaching an occurrence to an existing record is available and deliberate; filing a new record stays the cheap default. That asymmetry is the clause, not a preference: a duplicate is visible and cheap to triage, while a wrong merge makes a distinct defect vanish and the count lie, so the tool must never make the merge the path of least resistance — least of all for an agent that has just hit the friction and is the worst placed to classify it.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 5: Fault `nobody` is never counted as a defect, and **absence of a fault is never read as one**. The query reports `nobody`, because a question nobody could have answered is real information about where knowledge was missing, and excludes it from every count and rate presented as a defect measure. Reporting and counting are different acts and this clause turns on the difference. A record predating the field is reported in its own **unclassified** bucket and excluded from those same rates — never folded into `nobody`, which would look like a small convenience and would empty the value of the meaning the whole axis depends on. Unclassified is a reported category, not a fourth fault: fault stays exactly tooling, contract or nobody, and absence stays absence. They are not backfilled — 76 live records carry no fault, the number falls as they close, and guessing one for a record whose author is gone is how `nobody` becomes the catch-all.
deliverable: Fault `nobody` is never counted as a defect, and **absence of a fault is never read as one**. The query reports `nobody`, because a question nobody could have answered is real information about where knowledge was missing, and excludes it from every count and rate presented as a defect measure. Reporting and counting are different acts and this clause turns on the difference. A record predating the field is reported in its own **unclassified** bucket and excluded from those same rates — never folded into `nobody`, which would look like a small convenience and would empty the value of the meaning the whole axis depends on. Unclassified is a reported category, not a fourth fault: fault stays exactly tooling, contract or nobody, and absence stays absence. They are not backfilled — 76 live records carry no fault, the number falls as they close, and guessing one for a record whose author is gone is how `nobody` becomes the catch-all.
evidence:
The rate section is right and mutation-proven; the exclusion the query prints is broader
than the exclusion it performs, and the gap lands on the axis this clause exists to protect. Proven
right: `printRates` (friction.ts:63-68) counts only `DEFECT_FAULTS = ['tooling','contract']`, and both
attacks on it die — `c5-nobody-counted-as-a-defect` (DEFECT_FAULTS widened to include 'nobody') and
`c5-absence-folded-into-nobody` (`bucketOf`'s `?? 'unclassified'` changed to `?? 'nobody'`, the one
substitution the clause names as the small convenience that would empty the axis) are each KILLED by
`friction.test.ts > c1, c5, c7, c8, c10, c12: one query over the channel > reports nobody and
unclassified, and counts neither as a defect`, both re-run at that file with the mutation still applied.
What fails: `BUCKET_NOTE` (friction.ts:28-33) prints "Reported, and counted in nothing below" for
`nobody` and "Counted in nothing below" for `unclassified`, and both are then counted below. Reproduced
live on an isolated store — `npm run tasks -- add "nobody could have known this lesson applied" --id
nobody-breach --kind finding --fault nobody --severity low --deliverable "record it" --breaches
worker/mutation-proof --store <scratch>` then `tasks recur nobody-breach --note "..."` then `tasks
friction --store <scratch>` prints, in one run: `nobody 1 record(s) ... Reported, and counted in nothing
below`, then `1 recurrence(s) recorded against 1 record(s)`, then `worker/mutation-proof  1 record(s),
1 further occurrence(s) — nobody-breach`. The nobody-fault record and its occurrence are counted twice
below the line that says they are counted in nothing. `printByLesson` (friction.ts:112-113) filters on
`task.breaches.includes(lesson.id)` over every reporting record with no fault filter at all, and
`printOccurrences` (friction.ts:88) totals occurrences the same way, so an `unclassified` record carrying
occurrences reaches the same two counts by the same code path. This is not a mislabelled line only: the
spec's own Deliverable says the breach axis "turns 'how many defects' into 'which lesson is not landing',
which is the actionable form", so the per-lesson section is the defect reading restated, and c5's
sentence is that `nobody` is excluded from every count presented as a defect measure. Graded unmet
rather than deferred because the harm the spec states for getting this wrong — "counting it creates
pressure to write specs that pretend to know what they cannot" — is the reason the axis exists, and the
fix is small: filter both sections the way `printRates` already does, or narrow the printed promise to
name the one section it is true of.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 8: Every count is presented with the denominator it is a rate over, drawn from events the log already carries rather than from a new tally anyone has to maintain. A bare count cannot answer "how well is the system working", and a denominator that is itself hand-kept is a second thing to drift.
deliverable: Every count is presented with the denominator it is a rate over, drawn from events the log already carries rather than from a new tally anyone has to maintain. A bare count cannot answer "how well is the system working", and a denominator that is itself hand-kept is a second thing to drift.
evidence:
Every count does arrive beside a denominator, and no denominator is a hand-kept tally —
but one of the three denominators is not the quantity it is labelled as, and the count is inside it, so
the rate it presents cannot mean what it says. Measured on the real store: `npm run tasks -- friction`
prints `57 against 299 audit passes (audit events) — 19 per 100`. There are not 299 audit passes.
`grep -c '"op":"audit"' docs/events.jsonl` is 299; `grep '"op":"audit"' docs/events.jsonl | grep -c
'"id":null'` is 72, and `grep '"op":"audit"' docs/events.jsonl | grep -vc '"id":null'` is 227. `tasks
audit` emits one `audit` event for the pass (`audit.ts:553-556`, `id: null`) plus one per finding the
pass filed, and the findings-only route emits one per finding with no pass event at all
(`audit.ts:414`). So the denominator is 4x the quantity it names, and — worse — the 227 finding events
are the same findings the numerator counts, so filing a defect-fault finding increments both sides of
its own rate. Reproduced from empty: one `tasks audit demo-spec --proof ... --finding ...` on an
isolated store produced `2 audit passes (audit events)` and the query printed `2 against 2 audit passes
— 100 per 100` after one pass. Nothing in the suite pins this: mutation
`c8-audit-denominator-counts-only-real-passes`, which *corrects* the denominator to
`.filter((event) => event.id === null)`, SURVIVED at every scope up to the whole suite (0 failed of
2040) — the right answer and the wrong one are indistinguishable to the tests. The other two
denominators are sound and pinned: `c8-a-bare-count-with-no-denominator` (the rate loop replaced by a
bare count) and `c8-dispatch-denominator-drawn-from-the-wrong-op` (`start` swapped for `add`) are each
KILLED by `friction.test.ts > ... > presents every count beside the denominator it is a rate over,
drawn from the log`, re-run at that file with the mutation applied. The fix is the filter the surviving
mutation already spells, plus a test that asserts the number rather than only its presence; the clause
is a promise about what a denominator *is*, and a denominator containing its own numerator is the one
shape a rate must not have.

title: 470 of the 471 reporting-kind records in the store carry no fault, and nothing says what the channel query does with them

Either is a decision the query's worker should make on purpose rather than discover on the first run.
evidence: Counting the store at e9218fd: 471 records of kind finding or question, of which 470 carry fault null and exactly one carries a fault. normalizeTask keeps null distinct from nobody on purpose and friction.test.ts pins it, which is right. But c2's stated purpose is that no route can produce a record the query has to guess about, and on the day the query is written 99.8 percent of the channel is exactly that. The deliverable of one-query-over-the-channel-and-the-second-place-retired names grouping by fault, the nobody exclusion and the three denominators, and says nothing about a null fault, so the query's worker will meet this with no ruling. Grouped by fault, the channel's first report is one contract record and 470 blanks.

title: Citation matching is pinned exact on four axes and unpinned on whitespace and the empty string

evidence:
Two mutations survived the whole suite, 1783 tests, having changed behaviour.
lh-find-trims-whitespace made findLesson fall back to `LESSONS_BY_ID.get(id.trim())`, so
' worker/mutation-proof ' resolves to a live lesson — the silent mis-attribution the worker's own
decision note calls strictly worse than the silent drop this clause refuses. lh-unknown-drops-the-
empty-citation added `id !== '' &&` to unknownLessonIds' filter, so an empty citation stops being
reported — exactly the silent drop, at the reporting function, for the one input its sibling is
tested on: briefLessons.test.ts:71 pins findLesson('') to undefined and nothing pins
unknownLessonIds(['']). This is the neighbour rather than the finding the worker already fixed:
the property is that the match is exact and total, and it is currently held by tests on case
(line 77), truncation (line 75), suffix (line 76) and prefix (line 92) alone. The next branch is

title: mutate reports KILLED when a flaky test fails in the mutated run but not in the baseline, and names no test, so a flake is indistinguishable from proof
deliverable: A KILLED verdict names the tests that failed, so a reader can see whether the failure is in the mutation's neighbourhood before accepting it as proof. That is the cheap half and it also serves the check the auditor brief already demands, that a mutation fail for the right reason. Optionally the whole-suite rung re-runs a scope once before declaring KILLED, since baseline subtraction cannot help against an intermittent failure.
evidence: In this audit, breaking scripts/lib/taskStore.ts "!DECIDERS.includes(decider as Decider)" to "false" reported KILLED, 2 failed of 1786, at the whole-suite rung. An identical re-run of the same mutation minutes later reported SURVIVED, 0 failed of 1786, and a third whole-suite run in the same session reported "1 test(s) were already failing before this mutation". npm test is green and npm run tasks -- merge-ready passes. verdictOf already subtracts the baseline's failures, which handles a tree that is red every time; it cannot handle a test that is red on one roll and green on the next, which is what the open record npm-test-flakes-on-three-slow-spawn-heavy-tests-under-full-suite-contention describes. A KILLED verdict is what a clause is graded met on, so this manufactures proof rather than merely wasting a run. It cost this audit two whole-suite runs to notice.

title: Nothing in the dispatch machinery reads a question's decider, so work-prompt hands a worker an implementation brief for a question addressed to the author
deliverable: The commands that dispatch read Task.decider instead of only printing it. work-prompt on a kind question prints a decision brief - the question, its evidence, the records it holds up, and the two verbs that close it - rather than the implementation brief, and next and start name the addressee before offering or claiming the record. That is what makes the addressee the point rather than a label on it, which is the distinction c4 draws itself.
evidence: Reproduced against a scratch store on this branch: tasks add "held work" --id held-work --spec demo-spec; tasks question "Which way?" --blocks held-work --decider author --fault nobody; tasks done free-work; then tasks work-prompt which-way prints "You are implementing which-way on branch ...", "Correct the grant: npm run tasks -- edit which-way --writes ...", "Register any durable capability this produces", and "Then work: commit after each logical chunk, and close with npm run tasks -- done which-way --commit HEAD". tasks start which-way --actor worker-a claims it with no mention of the addressee, and tasks next offers it to whoever runs it. grep -rn "\.decider" over scripts/ returns render.ts:62 and records.ts:781 as the only readers, both of them printers. The failure c4 exists to prevent is an escalation whose only routes are ruling or stalling; today the escalation route loops back to the worker as work to implement.

title: The dedupe filter in cmdQuestion guards a case that cannot arise, so its predicate can never be false
deliverable: Drop the filter and use blocked directly, letting held and blocked be one list. The two names imply a distinction that the id's construction rules out, and a guard that cannot fire reads to the next reader as a case that has been handled.
evidence: The id is built by uniqueId(slugify(title), taken) where taken is every id already in the store, so no existing record's requires can contain it and "!task.requires.includes(id)" is true for every element of blocked. Replacing "blocked.filter((task) => !task.requires.includes(id))" with "blocked.filter(() => true)" SURVIVED the whole suite, 0 failed of 1786, which is the correct result for a no-op rather than a coverage gap.

title: The lessons table takes every `tasks` read down with it when one id is duplicated
deliverable:
Keep the throw inside indexLessons, which is a pure function refusing malformed
input at the point the ids become keys. Drop the eager module-scope call — build the map on first
findLesson call — so that only a command actually resolving a citation can fail, and every other
read still answers. The shipped table's distinctness is already proven without any module-load
work by briefLessons.test.ts:113-115, which asserts the nineteen ids are distinct, and CI runs it.
evidence:
briefLessons.ts:151 runs `const LESSONS_BY_ID = indexLessons(allLessons())` at module
scope, and indexLessons throws on a duplicate id. scripts/tasks/commands.ts:4 imports audit.ts,
which imports briefLessons.ts, so that line executes on every `tasks` invocation. Measured, not
reasoned: I duplicated one id ('auditor/silent-guess' set to 'auditor/next-neighbour'), and
`tasks doctor`, `tasks list` and `tasks next` all died with a Node stack trace instead of
answering, then restored the file from bytes captured before the edit. docs/workflow.md:169-170
says "Reads always answer; writes refuse only malformed input", and CLAUDE.md says doctor "fails
on one condition only: a docs/tasks.jsonl line that will not parse" — doctor now has a second, and
it is the diagnostic an agent reaches for precisely when something is already broken. The
condition deserves a refusal and the worker is right that a duplicate id is malformed input rather
than a semantic disagreement; the placement is what is wrong, because the same sentence that
licenses the refusal also promises the read.

title: The store's value-vocabulary guards in normalizeTask are untested as a class, not only the two this branch added
deliverable: One test that feeds normalizeTask a store line carrying an out-of-vocabulary value for each of grant, fault and decider and asserts the StoreError names the field, so the class is covered by construction rather than a guard at a time. Stated as a boundary rather than a list: every enumerated field normalizeTask validates gets a line in that test when it is added.
evidence: Breaking "!FAULTS.includes(fault as Fault)" to "false" SURVIVED the whole suite, 0 failed of 1786. So did "!DECIDERS.includes(decider as Decider)" on a clean re-run. No test anywhere in scripts/ asserts that an invalid enumerated value in a store line is refused.

title: A second prose friction channel is still tracked under the directory this branch retired, and the guard that should catch it names one filename

title: c8's audit denominator counts every finding an audit filed as if it were an audit pass, so the rate contains its own numerator
deliverable: Count only the pass events in c8's audit denominator — `filterEvents(events, { op: 'audit' }).filter((event) => event.id === null).length` — and assert the number rather than its presence, so the denominator is the quantity its label names and does not contain its own numerator.

Nothing pins it: the mutation that *corrects* the denominator to count only `id: null` events SURVIVED at every scope up to the whole suite, 0 failed of 2040.

title: `nobody` and `unclassified` print as counted in nothing, and are then counted in the recurrence total and the per-lesson breach count

title: `tasks audit` and `tasks import` file a finding without showing what already claims its path, which is how a third of the channel arrived
deliverable: Call the two lines `cmdAdd` already runs — `offerRecurrence(task, reportPriorArtOnPaths(config, tasks, task))` — from `cmdAudit`'s finding route and from `cmdImport`, after each saves the store, so a finding filed through an audit shows what already claims its path and is offered the occurrence. `priorArt` is an existing query; this is wiring, as the clause says.
evidence: Reproduced live on an isolated store: `tasks add "first sighting..." --kind finding --fault tooling --files scripts/tasks/audit.ts:88` printed the full `prior art on scripts/tasks/audit.ts` block; `tasks audit demo-spec --proof 1=met --evidence 1=checked --proof 2=met --evidence 2=checked --finding "second sighting..." --fault tooling --deliverable "generate it" --evidence "ten minutes again" --file scripts/tasks/audit.ts:88` printed `1 finding(s) recorded, unreviewed` and nothing else. Both records sit in the store carrying `"files":["scripts/tasks/audit.ts:88"]` and the second author was never shown the first. `grep -n "priorArt\|reportPriorArt" scripts/tasks/audit.ts` is empty. Scale: 227 of the 603 reporting-kind records in `docs/tasks.jsonl` carry both a `source` and a non-empty `files` list, so more than a third of the channel was filed blind — through the one route the generated auditor brief tells auditors to use.

title: The c9 and c12 refusals are guarded by a text scan over one file, and three walk-arounds survive the whole suite
deliverable: Guard the two refusals by the property rather than by one file's source text: assert over every file the gate reaches (doctor.ts and planCheck.ts are legs of it) and over comparisons rather than inequalities, or drop the text scan and pin the behaviour — that a store full of fault-null findings and recurring breaches still exits zero through `merge-ready`, `doctor` and `plan`.
evidence: Three mutations, all SURVIVED at every scope up to the whole suite (0 failed of 2040). `c9-an-exit-code-reads-a-fault` widened doctor's exit condition to `dangling > 0 || tasks.some((task) => task.kind === 'finding' && task.fault === null)`, making a merge-ready leg and a CI check exit on a fault; `mergeReady.test.ts`'s c9 describe is a `not.toContain` scan over `mergeReady.ts` alone and cannot see it. `c12-a-threshold-written-without-an-inequality` added `if (occurrenceCount.size === 3) console.log('three lessons are recurring — escalating this to a planner')` to `printByLesson`; `friction.test.ts:716`'s regex bans `.length >` and `count >` but not `=== `. `c12-a-threshold-outside-the-one-file-the-guard-reads` added `if (occurrences.length >= 3) console.log('... it is now scheduled work')` to `cmdRecur` in records.ts; the guard reads friction.ts only, while c12 says "anywhere in any code path". title: c12's stated rule is wrong in both directions: six count-threshold shapes walk around it, four of them proven to survive the whole suite, and it bans the invariant c5's own text states
deliverable:
Delete the regex and keep the behavioural test, extended. A source-text scan
  cannot express "no count decides anything", and the evidence that it cannot is that the rule
  has now been rewritten once against three reproductions and immediately walked around by
  four more. The test that does hold the property already exists in the same describe block:
  extend "says nothing more about a lesson breached four times than about one breached once" to
  the other things a count could decide, an exit code, an ordering, a filter and a dispatch
  position, and let the regex go rather than growing its vocabulary a third time. Deleting it
  loses nothing the behavioural test does not cover, and it stops certifying a refusal it
  cannot detect.
evidence:
Four mutations, each an elevation the rule permits, all SURVIVED at every scope up
  to the whole suite, 0 failed of 2056. Compared to a named constant:
  `const NOT_LANDING = 3; if (counted.length >= NOT_LANDING)` in printByLesson, where the rule
  requires a digit after the operator. Compared to another count:
  `if (recurrences > counted.length)`, which contains no literal at all. Reached through a call
  rather than a bare field: `if (cited.filter(isDefect).length >= 3)`, where `.filter(...)`
  separates the vocabulary word from `.length`, in friction.ts, a file the scan does read. And
  in a file the scan does not read: `if (breaches.length >= 3)` printed into the worker and
  planner brief from workPrompt.ts, which already imports loadEvents and filterEvents, so the
  elevation is the one line the clause says it is, and it lands in the brief a planner actually

  probed with `npm run inspect` over the exact regex: `FAULTS.length === 3` is BANNED, and that

title: c9 and c12 are still stated as sentences their own implementation contradicts, and this branch added a fourth contradiction after pass 3 recommended restating them
deliverable:

evidence:

title: The workflow records what cost it in one place, with one query over it
deliverable: One channel for recording what working the process cost, one query over it, and nothing else keeping a parallel copy. Classify on both axes so a planner can ask 'what should we fix in the tooling' and 'how should we plan differently' separately, and pair the count with its denominator - specs written, clauses authored, work-prompts issued - because 'how well is the system working' is a rate and a bare count cannot answer it. Retire .planning/agent-feedback/tool-friction.md and rewrite audit-prompt's step 8 to file into the channel instead, so the second system stops being generated by the tool. A record whose fault is 'nobody, the knowledge did not exist' must NOT count as a defect: counting it creates pressure to write specs that pretend to know what they cannot. THIRD ELEMENT, added 2026-08-06 after briefs-carry-the-lessons landed nineteen instructions in the four generated briefs: a record may name the LESSON it breaches. That turns the question from 'how many defects' into 'which lesson is not landing', which is the actionable one - a lesson breached repeatedly is badly worded, in the wrong brief, or wrong, and each of those is fixable by editing one line. The information mostly exists already, since an auditor finding a test that cannot fail IS a breach of a worker lesson and a fix-the-neighbour instance IS a breach of an auditor lesson; what is missing is the link. Pair it with a CHECKED-AND-CLEAN marker, because a lesson with zero breaches is ambiguous between 'it works' and 'nobody looked', and the audit brief already distinguishes these by telling auditors that none-found is real only if they looked. Do not gate on any of it: counting breaches while penalising them creates pressure not to report them, which costs the only honest signal there is.
evidence: Author's observation 2026-08-06: tool friction and spec defects are the same shape - log a problematic event so a future session can plan work against it - and should not be two systems. Confirmed, and the fragmentation already exists in the tooling rather than being something the two proposed tasks would introduce. (1) audit.ts:642 step 8 and audit.ts:1148 tell every auditor to log friction as dated prose in .planning/agent-feedback/tool-friction.md - a tracked markdown file outside the store, unqueryable, unclassified, uncounted, and with a known past finding that only one of two auditors followed it. (2) The event log, where this session has been recording spec defects and friction as op note and op decision with the class inside prose. (3) Task records, where a defect worth fixing becomes a finding. The two tasks this replaces would have made four. UNIFIED MODEL, two orthogonal axes rather than a flat class list: does it STOP WORK (blocking, which is level 2 - the spec is incoherent and work halts - versus non-blocking, level 1 - obvious remedy, worker continues), and WHAT IS AT FAULT (the tooling, so a future session fixes a command; the contract, so a future session plans differently; or nobody, because the knowledge did not exist when the spec was written). Blocking needs no new machinery: isBlocked is waitingOn().length > 0 and requirementStates releases on both done and declined, so a record named in the spec members' requires halts dispatch and answering or dismissing it unblocks. Kind 'question' already exists in the Kind union, in KINDS, accepted by tasks add at records.ts:103, and is used by ZERO records - a declared noun with no behaviour, which is where this belongs.
reason: Decomposed into spec the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place and three slices over disjoint write regions. Same disposition as tool-friction-backlog and for the same reason: its forecast grant named six files spanning all three slices, so it collides with every one of them, and its produces claim on 'process friction channel' now duplicates the slice that actually builds it. Nothing in it is dropped. Its deliverable is the spec's Deliverable, its two recorded judgements are the spec's Decisions, and its three elements land as clauses: the two axes as c2 and c3, the fault-nobody rule as c5, the lesson breach as c6 with its checked-and-clean pair as c7, the denominator as c8, and the never-gate rule as c9. What the decomposition adds beyond the record: c4, a blocking question's third route, which is the remedy for run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks c3 and was not visible until that run failed the clause and the audit said why.

title: Close the tool-friction backlog, starting with prior-art discovery
evidence: One task for the whole of .planning/agent-feedback/tool-friction.md plus the planning-session friction of 2026-08-04. Leads with the gap that cost the most: there is no way to ask whether a thing already exists. produces catches a duplicate only when both sides spell the capability the same way, so it caught 'buff engine' and missed 'per expression' against combat-events' '+N <stat> per <counter>' — one grammar, two owners, surfaced only as a stats.ts write collision that had to be interpreted.
