Single-session items: merge-ready answers repo health but not branch standing, so a merge needs six manual reads and does not fail when main has moved; merge-ready prints 'every leg passed' over doctor warnings whose whole subject is work about to be lost; tasks show does not surface what tasks note recorded, so a close says that it closed and never why; spec show refuses the slug next infers; a store query from another branch answers 0 rather than refusing, because the store is silently ref-scoped; three flag shapes for an id (spec add --id, add --note); audit-status is an npm script surrounded by tasks verbs; probe --each names documents stdin[3], which is not a legal module id, so a variant that loads clean reports as broken; tasks decision loses to commit bodies because the commit has a writing prompt attached and the store does not. Its own grant was scripts/tasks/ and scripts/lib/ whole, which collides with every slice beneath it; the backlog narrative it carried is now the spec's Deliverable and the slices' evidence.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 19: A worker's brief is generated, never hand-written, the way an auditor's already is. The one instruction that dispatches a worker is `run npm run tasks -- work-prompt <id> and do what it says` — symmetric with the auditor's, and for the same reason CLAUDE.md gives for that one: a hand-written brief is a copy of the record that drifts from it, and composing one is where a planner smuggles in detail nobody asked it to hold. The brief derives from the store and the spec what the record already knows — the task's deliverable and evidence, its write grant, its `produces` forecast, what it requires and whether those are closed, the proof clauses it discharges and their current standing, the files the grant resolves to — and adds the three obligations `docs/workflow.md` puts on a worker before it writes code: claim the record, correct the grant against what it actually finds, and register any durable capability. It ends by inviting refusal, because a grant made by a planner that has not read the region is a forecast and the worker is the first party in the workflow able to say so. Among what it prints is one line of provenance — the branch this spec was last written from, read off the event log — because one spec is one branch, so a worktree cut from `main` after the first member has landed reads a store that looks current while missing what the branch has closed. It states the fact and stops: no comparison against the current branch, no reset command, no environment repair. Whoever dispatches a worker already knows which branch the work is on, and a line they can check against costs three lines over `loadEvents` and `filterEvents`, which exist and are tested.

title: two proof targets name behaviour their tests do not assert, so a green run reports more than it checked
deliverable: `leaves no file behind` (c14) drives `compile` + `loaderFor` in process and asserts a non-recursive `readdirSync(repoRoot)` is unchanged; neither function contains a filesystem write, so no implementation of them could fail it, and a write into a subdirectory would be missed. `records a whole pass from a file, and a flag typed beside it still wins` (c13, scripts/tasks.test.ts:4473) asserts the first half and nothing about precedence. Fixing them means asserting the named behaviour -- spawn the CLI and check `git status --porcelain`, and pass `--base-branch` both in the file and beside `--args-from` -- or narrowing the names to what is checked. This is the pass-1 HIGH one step in: a target that resolves to a test that cannot fail is a green run that asserted nothing.
evidence: scripts/inspect.ts imports only `readFileSync` from node:fs and writes nothing; `run()` in scripts/inspect.test.ts:8 calls compile+loaderFor directly rather than spawning `tsx scripts/inspect.ts`, so the assertion is over two pure functions. For the c13 target, `grep -n "args-from" scripts/tasks.test.ts` returns three lines, all inside the two tests at 4473 and 4487, and neither passes a flag both in the file and on the command line; the ordering that implements it is `parseAuditArgs([...fromFile.argv, ...fromFile.rest])` at scripts/tasks/audit.ts:502.

title: `unresolvedTarget` matches the whole test file, so a proof target naming any string in it -- an assertion argument or a comment -- is reported as resolved while `vitest -t` skips every test and exits 0
deliverable: The check installed to stop pass 1's HIGH from recurring has a false negative in the direction that matters: it says a bad target is fine. Match against title positions only -- the string literal in an `it(`/`test(`/`describe(` call, which is what the function's own comment says it is doing -- instead of `unescaped(text).includes(unescaped(name))` over the raw file. Fixing it means a drifted target is caught by the one command that reads proofTargets, which is the whole reason the check was added.
evidence: Reproduced through `npm run inspect`, calling `unresolvedTarget` directly: `vitest scripts/tasks/mergeReady.test.ts "main has moved past the merge base"` returns null (resolved), because that string is the argument of an `expect(...).toContain(...)` at scripts/tasks/mergeReady.test.ts:110, not a test title. `npx vitest run scripts/tasks/mergeReady.test.ts -t "main has moved past the merge base"` then reports "Test Files 1 skipped (1), Tests 13 skipped (13)" and exits 0 -- exactly the failure the pass-1 HIGH described. Second reproduction: `vitest scripts/tasks.test.ts "A target naming a test that does not exist is worse than no target"` also returns null, matching a comment at scripts/tasks.test.ts:4410. The collision is not contrived here: this repo writes long sentences as both test titles and assertion arguments, and copies clause prose into test-file comments verbatim, so an invented target drawn from clause prose has a real chance of matching one. All five existing tests of unresolvedTarget (scripts/tasks.test.ts:4414-4442) exercise a two-line fixture in which every string is a title, so none of them can see this.

title: Which candidate a boundary's source names is unasserted for buff, action and requested time
deliverable: Either make nextBoundary's attribution observable without widening the barrel — a seam the ruling of 2026-08-07 allows — or record that the three unreachable candidates are deliberately unasserted, so the survivors stop reading as an open hole.

What remains is the wiring: mutating buffKey: key -> 'something', ownerRef: active.ownerRef -> 'something', and the initial source { kind: 'requested' } -> a buff source all SURVIVED at whole-suite scope, 0 failed of 1817. They survive because those three candidates cannot reach either guard from engine-produced state — applyDueBoundaries deletes every buff with expiresAt <= now before each nextBoundary call, and the action and requested instants are built at or after state.time — so only a resource boundary is observable through resolve(), and it is asserted twice. title: work-prompt does not carry the comment policy, so every worker rediscovers it or violates it
deliverable: Put CLAUDE.md's comment rule in the generated worker brief, in the same spirit as the tool-friction and grant-correction instructions it already carries. The two clauses that actually bite are 'never describe another module's contract' and 'never close an audit finding by writing its rationale into the source' -- both are counter-intuitive to a competent engineer acting on normal instincts, which is exactly why the brief has to say them rather than assume them.
evidence: 2026-08-06, observed live on claude/task-store-parallel. Removing a dead tie-break, the worker left a four-line comment explaining why the two remaining sort terms suffice. It described listQueue's ordering -- another module's contract, forbidden by name -- and restated the rationale for closing a pass-2 finding, which CLAUDE.md forbids separately and which the commit message already carried better. The worker was not briefed on either rule: work-prompt prints the spec, clauses, grant and prior art, and says nothing about comments. This is not a worker defect; a reasonable engineer writes that comment. Fault is the brief. Cost: the coordinator caught it at merge, after two audit passes had already run without seeing it, because the comment landed after pass 2.
reason: Folded into lessons-say-what-the-run-learned. The scratchpad collision is fixed where it is caused: every generated brief that hands an agent a scratch path namespaces it per agent, so three auditors on three branches stop writing to one filename. Its own deliverable named that as the option -- tell dispatched agents to disambiguate -- and the brief is where a dispatched agent is told anything. The comment policy rides the same file set through work-prompt.

title: work-prompt refuses a spec slug, the one name a human actually knows
deliverable: npm run tasks -- work-prompt <spec-slug> resolves the spec and briefs its next unblocked member, or briefs the spec as a whole. A dispatcher knows the name of the work, not which member is currently unblocked; tasks next --spec <slug> already answers that in one call, so the refusal is holding the information the caller needs. This is the near-miss-refusal shape tool-friction-backlog closed for other verbs, and work-prompt was not one of them.
evidence: npm run tasks -- work-prompt audit-loop-costs-less prints 'no such task: audit-loop-costs-less' and five near-misses fuzzy-matched on task titles (pre-release-readiness-audit, four closed findings), none of which is the spec of that exact name in docs/specs/. The spec is ready, and tasks next --spec audit-loop-costs-less returns mutate-narrows-to-a-test unambiguously. The workaround is a root task whose id equals the slug, which 11 specs already carry; tool-friction-backlog was declined because that root task's write grant collided with every slice beneath it, so the workaround costs either a colliding grant or a record that exists only to satisfy a lookup. Secondary, and systemic rather than this verb's fault: show, work-prompt and audit-prompt all exit 0 on an unresolvable argument, so a dispatched agent has no signal beyond the text.

title: Generate a worker's brief
deliverable: Clause 19. tasks work-prompt <id> prints everything a worker needs, derived from the store and the spec: deliverable, evidence, write grant and the files it resolves to, produces forecast, requirements and whether they are closed, the clauses it discharges and their standings, the three workflow obligations before writing code (claim, correct the grant, register a concept), and an invitation to refuse the grant. It also prints one line of provenance, the branch this spec was last written from, read off the event log via loadEvents/filterEvents - three lines over helpers that already exist and take spec as a filter key. It states that fact and stops: no comparison against the current branch, no reset command, no node_modules repair. The single instruction that dispatches a worker becomes 'run npm run tasks -- work-prompt <id> and do what it says', symmetric with audit-prompt. Dispatch this slice FIRST - every other member is then dispatched through it.
evidence: This planning session was about to hand-write a dispatch brief, which is the defect: CLAUDE.md says the auditor's brief is generated and never hand-written, and there is no counterpart for a worker. The provenance line is worth having because one spec is one branch, so a worktree cut from main after the first member lands reads a store that looks current while missing what the branch closed - silent, not empty. It stops at the fact because whoever spawns a worktree owns that environment and already knows the branch. Measured: loadEvents, eventsPathFor and filterEvents are exported from scripts/lib/eventLog.ts, covered by eventLog.test.ts, and filterEvents already takes spec; git reset --hard <branch> needs no path, so the git-common-dir subprocess and the Windows-only mklink that an earlier scoping attached here buy nothing.

title: WORKER_LESSONS has no instruction to aim a fix at the clause, so the workflow detects too-small fixes instead of preventing them
deliverable: The measured durability rate says the fix is the decision this workflow gets wrong: within the orchestrated run, one set of auditors under one set of briefs reversed 0 of 84 certifications and got 6 of 10 fixes wrong. The instruction that addresses it exists and is in the WRONG LIST. AUDITOR_LESSONS 2 says 'Hunt the next neighbour, not confirmation of the last fix - a finding names one reproduction, and the reproduction is always narrower than the property the clause promises.' That tells an auditor to CATCH a too-small fix. Nothing tells a worker not to MAKE one: WORKER_LESSONS' four entries cover comments, tests that cannot fail, recording silent decisions, and filing what you notice outside your grant. The orchestrator that watched all three branches wrote the missing sentence down at 18:35:31Z - 'a fix should be aimed at the clause rather than at the finding' - as one of two remedies, and only the auditor half was carried into briefLessons.ts. Add the worker half.
evidence: Measured over 24 specs, 55 passes, 470 clause gradings; method and exclusions in the note event of 2026-08-06 against one-query-over-the-channel-and-the-second-place-retired. Repository-wide the fix failure rate is 30.4 percent (7 of 23) against a certification reversal rate of 0.5 percent (2 of 428). Every one of the seven failures is a fix aimed at a finding's literal words: a-clause-can-be-deferred c2 three times, where three successive narrowings each swapped one hand-picked character list for a longer one; every-triage c4 twice and c6 once; audit-loop-costs-less c5 once. Detecting these costs an extra audit pass each time, which is the cheapest possible way to catch them and still more expensive than not making them. Filed rather than fixed: briefLessons.ts is the grant of a-lesson-has-a-handle-that-survives-rewording-it, whose job is handles and not content.
reason: Folded whole into lessons-say-what-the-run-learned. All three are content in the brief lesson tables, all three were filed rather than fixed because briefLessons.ts was another task's grant, and that task -- a-lesson-has-a-handle-that-survives-rewording-it -- merges immediately before this one. Fixing them in three branches would mean three rewrites of one file for changes that share a reviewer's single reading. The orchestrator-records finding contributes only its free half, the rule that a worker never cites an id it cannot resolve; where an orchestrator files during a parallel run stays open as a planning question for whenever the freeze lifts, since no parallel run happens during it.

title: Retire workflow.md's numbered steps into the commands that enact them, and keep only the why
deliverable: Once work-prompt tells a worker what it owes (c19) and merge-ready names the next move at every leg (c18), the 11 numbered steps of docs/workflow.md are a second copy of what the tool says at the moment it matters. Retire the procedure half. Keep 'Advice that is known good' and 'Why it is shaped this way': a command that re-explains write grants, concepts and audit-output asymmetry on every invocation is noise, and reasoning that lives only in code rots. Needs a planning session, not an implementer - what survives is a judgement about which sentences are protocol and which are rationale.
evidence: Raised 2026-08-04 while scoping c18/c19/c20. Not a full retirement: CLAUDE.md's rule is that when the tool and workflow.md disagree, that is a defect in one of them, which is a two-sided invariant - delete the document and the tool becomes self-certifying, whatever it prints being the workflow by definition. That is the same failure the comment-budget gate showed when it certified commits that deleted CI steps. So the procedure half is genuinely redundant once the commands guide, and the reasoning half is what makes drift detectable at all.
